policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, volunteers and governing authority members with access to patient information
policies.purpose: To protect the confidentiality of patient information in every form and to meet the New York home care regulations and the federal HIPAA Privacy, Security and Breach Notification Rules.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps every patient's record confidential. Patients may refuse release of their records to anyone outside the agency, except on transfer to a health care facility, as required by law, or under a third-party payment contract (10 NYCRR §766.1(a)(11)). The agency maintains written policies that safeguard records against loss or unauthorized access and govern their use, removal and release (§766.6(e)). Electronic records are secure from unwarranted access and can be printed on request for the agency and DOH (§766.12(b)). The agency complies with HIPAA, including its minimum necessary, notice of privacy practices, patient access and breach notification requirements. Employee health records are kept separate from the personnel file and treated with the same confidentiality as patient records. Criminal history results are used only for the purposes authorized by law.

definitions.definition: Individually identifiable health information about a patient, in any form (paper, electronic or oral), held by the agency.
The standard that staff use, disclose or request only the PHI needed for the task.
An acquisition, access, use or disclosure of PHI not permitted by HIPAA that compromises its security or privacy, unless a risk assessment shows a low probability of compromise.
The person designated by the Operator to develop and oversee privacy policies and receive privacy complaints. [PRIVACY OFFICER NAME].

procedures: The Operator designates a Privacy Officer and a Security Officer (who may be the same person) in writing and lists them in the Notice of Privacy Practices.

At intake, the agency gives each patient the Notice of Privacy Practices, asks for a signed acknowledgment of receipt, and documents the effort if the patient declines. The notice explains the patient's rights and the agency's duties.

Staff may access only the PHI needed for their job. Aides see the plan of care and task sheet for their assigned patients only. Access is role based and reviewed at least annually by the Privacy Officer.

Before releasing any record to someone outside the agency, staff verify the identity of the requester and check for a signed patient authorization, unless release is to a health care facility on transfer, required by law, or made under a third-party payment contract. Patients' refusals of release are honored and documented.

Disclosures to DOH, the MLTC plan, and the Medicaid program for survey, payment and oversight purposes are made through the RN Director of Patient Services or Operator, and limited to what is requested.

Paper records are kept in locked cabinets in the office, and charts are removed from the office only with the RN Director's approval, logged out and logged back in. Records left in a patient's home (such as the aide task sheet) are kept in a place agreed with the patient and not left where visitors can read them.

Electronic records require unique user IDs, strong passwords, automatic log-off, encryption of laptops, phones and portable media, audit logging, and regular backup. Staff do not share log-ins. Records can be printed on request for the agency and for DOH.

Employees do not discuss patients in public places, on social media, or with anyone without a work need. Photographs or recordings of patients or their homes are prohibited unless the patient has authorized them in writing.

When a patient or representative asks for a copy of the record, the Privacy Officer processes the request and provides access within 30 days, or sends a written extension notice as HIPAA allows. Patient requests for amendment or an accounting of disclosures are logged and answered within the HIPAA timelines.

All employees receive privacy and security training at orientation and annually, and sign a confidentiality agreement. Sanctions for violations, up to termination, are applied consistently and documented.

Employee health records, including immunization, TB screening and medical clearance, are kept in a locked file separate from the personnel file, with access limited to the Operator, RN Director of Patient Services and designated personnel staff (see PER-04, PER-05).
Criminal history record check results are kept confidential, are used only for the authorized employment-related purposes, and are not shared with unauthorized persons (see PER-02).

Any suspected privacy incident, such as a lost chart, a lost phone, a misdirected fax or email, or unauthorized access, is reported to the Privacy Officer immediately and no later than the end of the shift.

The Privacy Officer investigates within 2 business days, documents a risk assessment, and mitigates harm. If a breach of unsecured PHI occurred, the agency notifies affected patients without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery, notifies HHS as required (and the media where the rule applies), and reports in accordance with legal requirements and its contracts with MLTC plans.
When the agency discloses PHI to a vendor, such as billing, EVV or IT, the Operator first executes a business associate agreement. Agreements are kept on file and reviewed annually.

If the agency closes, the governing authority arranges storage of and access to records and notifies DOH in writing where they are kept (see REC-01). The Privacy Officer reviews this policy at least annually and after any breach (see GOV-03).

Oversees HIPAA compliance, manages access requests and breach investigations, and delivers training.
Controls release, removal and storage of clinical records.
Protect PHI, use the minimum necessary, and report incidents the same shift.

Signed patient authorizations and release logs

policies.title: Client Property, Gifts and Financial Exploitation Prevention
policies.applies_to: All employees, including personal care aides, supervisors and office staff; contractors
policies.purpose: To protect patients' property and money, treat them with dignity, and prevent financial exploitation by anyone serving on behalf of [AGENCY NAME].
policies.policy: Patients are treated with respect and recognition of their dignity and individuality, and complaints about lack of respect for a patient's property by anyone serving on the agency's behalf are handled under the complaint procedure (10 NYCRR §766.1(a)(9)-(10); see CR-02). Level I personal care tasks include shopping, bill payment and essential errands (18 NYCRR §505.14(a)(5)(i)), so the agency requires receipts and a documented record of any patient funds handled. Alleged theft and other accidents and incidents are documented in the patient record (§766.6(a)(8)). The rules in this policy on gifts, loans and money handling are standards adopted by the agency itself; they are not drawn from a specific Part 766 section. The agency is committed to preventing exploitation and to reporting suspected exploitation.

definitions.definition: Improper use of a patient's money, property, accounts or credit, including theft, forgery, coercion, undue influence or obtaining gifts, loans or bequests.
Anything of value, including cash, checks, jewelry, vehicles, property or loans, offered to an employee by a patient or the patient's family.
Cash or payment instruments belonging to the patient that an aide handles only to complete an assigned errand.

procedures: At orientation and annually, all staff are trained on this policy, on property respect, and on recognizing financial exploitation. Each signs an acknowledgment kept in the personnel file (see PER-03, PER-07).

Employees may not accept cash, checks, gifts of value, loans, or bequests from patients or families, may not ask to borrow money or property, and may not sell products or services to patients. Gifts of nominal value, such as a homemade snack, may be politely declined; if refusing would harm the patient, the employee reports it to the RN supervisor, who documents it.
Employees may not be named as beneficiary, power of attorney, health care proxy, executor or joint account holder for a patient, and may not witness legal or financial documents.

Aides may not hold, use or know the PIN of a patient's debit or credit card, or have access to the patient's bank accounts, checkbook, safe or valuables, except as the plan of care allows for an assigned errand.
When the plan of care assigns shopping, bill payment or other errands, the RN records the task, the amount authorized and the method of handling funds on the plan of care (see SVC-06, SAF-08).

For each errand using patient funds, the aide counts the money with the patient (or representative) before leaving, keeps all receipts, returns exact change and receipts, and has the patient sign the errand log. The aide never commingles patient funds with personal money.
Aides do not use a patient's car, phone, computer or property for personal purposes and do not remove any patient property from the home except as directed in writing for an agreed purpose.

At the start of services, the RN encourages the patient and family to put cash, jewelry and valuables in a secure place, and may advise them to keep an inventory. Staff do not take part in listing or storing valuables.
The RN reviews errand logs and receipts at each supervisory visit and compares them to the plan of care, looking for unexplained spending or missing items (see SVC-07).

Any employee who suspects theft, missing money or property, forged documents, coercion for gifts, or other financial exploitation reports it to the RN Director of Patient Services immediately, and within the same shift. The RN Director notifies the Operator and follows SAF-01. If a crime is suspected, the patient is told they may report to law enforcement, and the agency assists as appropriate.

The RN Director documents the report as an incident in the patient record, including the patient's statement, dates, items involved and actions taken (§766.6(a)(8); see SAF-02). Any theft allegation is also logged as a complaint if the patient or family raises it (CR-02).
The agency may remove the employee from the patient's case during the investigation. The agency does not retaliate against any person who reports a concern in good faith.

Substantiated violations lead to discipline up to termination and, where the law requires, report to the appropriate authorities and, where appropriate, to the Medicaid program or MLTC plan. The Operator reports potential fraud under GOV-05.
The QI Committee reviews exploitation, theft and property complaints and incident data at least quarterly (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Enforces this policy, decides disciplinary action, and makes outside reports.
Trains staff, reviews errand records, investigates reports and documents incidents.
Check errand logs and receipts at supervisory visits and watch for signs of exploitation.
Follow money-handling and gift rules, keep receipts, and report concerns immediately.

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors and volunteers; intake and admission staff; patients and applicants for service
policies.purpose: To make sure every person who seeks or receives services from [AGENCY NAME] is treated with respect and without discrimination, and that language or disability is never a barrier to understanding rights, services and care.
policies.policy: Each patient has the right to be treated with consideration, respect and full recognition of dignity and individuality (10 NYCRR §766.1(a)(10)). [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate in admission, care, scheduling, staffing or discharge on the basis of race, color, national origin, language, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, age, disability, marital status, immigration status, source of payment or any other protected characteristic. The agency provides rights information and payment information orally and in writing (§766.1(a)(3)(ii)) in a form the patient understands, including the patient's language, free of charge. The agency considers patient preferences and social and cultural considerations in care planning, consistent with the Medicaid personal care assessment and plan development requirements (18 NYCRR §505.14(b)). The agency's licensure application commits it to serve people who have difficulty obtaining care because of minority status, age, case complexity, payment source or location, and the agency acts in line with that commitment.

definitions.definition: A limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English well enough to take part in care.

A person who is fluent in English and the patient's language, trained in interpreting and bound by confidentiality. Family members and minors are not used except at the patient's informed request in an emergency or as the patient specifically chooses.
Services such as sign language interpreters, large print, braille, captioning or assistive technology that provide effective communication for people with disabilities.
A trait for which discrimination is prohibited by federal or New York law.

procedures: The governing authority adopts this policy, and the Operator posts a nondiscrimination notice in the office and includes it in the patient admission packet, in English and in the languages most common in the agency's service counties.

At intake, staff ask each patient (or representative) the preferred language for spoken and written communication and whether they need an aid for hearing, vision, speech, literacy or cognition. The answers are recorded in the clinical record.
The agency maintains a list of qualified interpreters and a telephone or video interpreter service available during all service hours. The Operator reviews the list and the vendor contract annually.

Interpretation and translation are free for patients. The agency does not require patients to bring their own interpreter and does not rely on children under 18. A family member or friend may interpret only if the patient requests it after being offered a qualified interpreter, and the choice is documented.

Rights information (CR-01), the statement of services and charges, the service agreement, the plan of care summary, complaint information (CR-02) and discharge notices are provided in the patient's language, or are read and interpreted aloud by a qualified interpreter, with the method documented in the record.
The agency matches aides to patients by language and cultural needs whenever practicable and as the patient prefers, and records this in the plan of care.

The RN considers the patient's preferences and social and cultural considerations (such as diet, religion, modesty and gender of caregiver) when developing and updating the plan of care, and documents them (see SVC-06).

Admission decisions are made only under the written acceptance criteria and the RN's determination that the agency can meet the patient's needs (see SVC-02). A person is never refused because of a protected characteristic, language, disability, immigration status or payment source. Any denial is documented with the clinical or capacity reason.

The agency provides reasonable accommodation for patients with disabilities, such as large-print documents, written communication for patients who are deaf or hard of hearing, accessible meeting locations, and modifications to procedures when needed to make services accessible.

Employees are trained on this policy at orientation and annually, including how to work with interpreters and how to avoid stereotyping or harassment (see PER-03). Employees may not make discriminatory or demeaning remarks to patients.

Staff who learn of discrimination or a language access failure report it to the RN Director of Patient Services the same day. Patients may also use the complaint procedure (CR-02) and may complain to the Department of Health or other civil rights agencies.
The RN Director of Patient Services investigates each report, takes corrective action, and records it in the complaint log. The agency does not retaliate against anyone who reports discrimination.
The QI Committee reviews language access data, such as requests for interpreters, translated documents and related complaints, at least annually (see GOV-04).
The Operator reviews the policy annually, along with the DOH policy and procedure review tool, and updates it when requirements change (see GOV-03).

Posts notices, contracts for interpreter services, and enforces the policy.
Ensures language and accommodation needs are assessed, documented and met, and investigates complaints.
Ask about language and communication needs and arrange interpreters.

policies.title: Service Agreement, Rates and Billing Disclosure
policies.applies_to: Intake staff, RN Director of Patient Services, billing staff, schedulers and all personnel who discuss services or charges with patients, families or payers
policies.purpose: To make sure every patient, and the patient's legally authorized representative, is told in advance and in writing what services are available, what they cost, who is expected to pay, and what the patient may have to pay. To make sure Medicaid and MLTC patients are never charged for services the plan authorizes.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will give each patient a written statement of available services and related charges before care starts. Before care starts, we will also explain orally and in writing how much payment is expected from third-party payers and how much the patient may have to pay. If any of this information changes, we will tell the patient orally and in writing within 30 calendar days of the date we learn of the change. We will make our charges and payment mechanisms available to the public. For Medicaid and MLTC patients, we will not bill the patient for any service the plan authorizes. We will record the plan's authorization (level, amount, frequency and duration) in the service agreement. We accept Medicaid or plan payment as payment in full for authorized covered services.

definitions.definition: The written document signed by the patient or representative and the agency that lists the services to be provided, the charges, the payer and the patient's financial responsibility.
Any payer other than the patient, including Medicaid, a Medicaid managed long term care (MLTC) plan, Medicare, long-term care insurance or another insurer.
The plan's or payer's approval of services, stating the level, amount, frequency and duration of services.
A person with legal authority to act for a patient who lacks capacity to exercise his or her rights.

procedures: The Administrator, with the RN Director of Patient Services, maintains a written schedule of services offered and a schedule of charges for private-pay patients. The Administrator approves each version and the effective date.
The Administrator keeps the services, charges and payment mechanisms available to the public (office, website and on request) so the public information requirements in GOV-02 are met.
At referral, the Intake Coordinator identifies the expected payer (Medicaid fee-for-service, MLTC plan, other insurer or private pay) and records it on the intake form.

Before the first visit, the Intake Coordinator gives the patient or representative the written statement of available services and related charges. The coordinator reviews it orally in the patient's preferred language (see CR-05).

Before the first visit, the Intake Coordinator explains orally and in writing the extent to which third-party payers are expected to pay and the extent to which the patient may have to pay. This includes any amount the plan or payer has said the patient owes, and the private-pay rate for any hours or services not authorized.

For Medicaid or MLTC patients, the Intake Coordinator obtains the plan's authorization before services begin. The authorization is attached to the service agreement, and the level, amount, frequency and duration are copied into the agreement.

The patient or representative signs the service agreement before care starts. The Intake Coordinator gives a copy to the patient and places the original in the clinical record. If the patient declines to sign, the coordinator documents the reason and notifies the RN Director of Patient Services.
The Intake Coordinator confirms the patient has received the written patient rights notice (see CR-01) at the same time and records the date in the clinical record.

Billing staff may bill the patient only for amounts disclosed in the signed service agreement. Billing staff may never bill a Medicaid or MLTC patient for any service the plan authorizes, or for any amount beyond what the plan or payer has determined the patient owes. Billing staff may not ask for a tip, gratuity or add-on fee.

If a Medicaid or MLTC patient asks for hours or services beyond the authorization, the Intake Coordinator tells the patient the additional services are not covered. The coordinator refers the request to the plan care manager and explains the patient's option to request a reassessment or to privately purchase additional services. Any private-pay arrangement is separate, written and signed before the additional service begins.

When a rate, payer, authorization, charge or payment responsibility changes, the person who learns of it notifies the Administrator the same business day. The Administrator logs the date the agency learned of the change.

Within 30 calendar days of the date the agency learned of a change, the Administrator or designee gives the patient or representative notice of the change orally and in writing. The notice is documented in the clinical record with the date, method and person giving the notice, and the service agreement is amended and signed.

Billing staff reconcile billing against authorizations each billing cycle. Any service billed outside the authorization, or any patient charge not supported by the signed agreement, is reported to the Administrator and corrected and refunded within the same billing cycle.
Patient questions or complaints about charges are handled under CR-02. The Administrator reviews billing complaints and reports patterns to the QI Committee (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the service and charge schedule, keeps charges and payment mechanisms public, receives change notices, and ensures the 30-day change notification is made.
Ensures the services listed in each agreement match the plan of care and the authorization.
Delivers and explains the service statement and payer information before care starts, obtains the signed agreement and attaches the authorization.
Bills only as disclosed and authorized, never bills Medicaid or MLTC patients for authorized services, and reconciles billing to authorizations.

policies.title: Scope of Services: What Personal Care Aides May and May Not Do
policies.applies_to: Personal care aides, RN Director of Patient Services, supervising RNs, schedulers and intake staff
policies.purpose: To define the tasks personal care aides may perform at Level I and Level II, to state what they may not do, and to ensure every aide works only within the plan of care and the authorization.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] aides perform only the tasks listed in the patient's plan of care and authorized by the plan or payer. Level I services are limited to nutritional and environmental support tasks. Level II services include Level I tasks plus personal care functions. Supervision and cueing are not standalone services. Advanced home health aide tasks are not offered unless the agency's license and the required RN supervision are in place. Patients may refuse advanced tasks, in which case an RN performs them. Any nursing or therapeutic service new to the agency goes to the QI Committee before it is offered.

definitions.definition: A person who meets the aide qualification and training requirements for a personal care aide under State law and who provides personal care services under RN supervision.
Nutritional and environmental support functions only. Authorization may not exceed 8 hours per week.
Level I tasks plus personal care functions such as bathing, dressing, toileting and transferring.

A task beyond routine personal care that may be delegated only to an appropriately qualified aide under RN supervision. [AGENCY NAME] does not offer these tasks unless its license and supervision arrangements are in place.

procedures: The RN Director of Patient Services maintains the approved task list for Level I and Level II and gives a copy to every aide at orientation (see PER-03).

Level I tasks aides may perform: making and changing beds; dusting and vacuuming rooms the patient uses; light cleaning of the kitchen, bedroom and bathroom; dishwashing; listing needed supplies; shopping when no other arrangements exist; laundry including ironing and mending; bill payment and essential errands; and meal preparation including simple modified diets.

Level II tasks aides may perform, in addition to Level I tasks: bathing; dressing; grooming; toileting; walking; transferring; turning and positioning; preparing modified-diet meals (low sugar, fat, salt or residue); feeding; supporting patient self-administration of medication (see SVC-08); routine skin care; using medical equipment such as walkers and wheelchairs; and changing simple dressings.
The RN who writes or reviews the plan of care lists only the authorized tasks, by Level, in the plan (see SVC-06). The aide receives a task sheet that reflects the plan.

An aide may not perform any task that is not in the plan of care, even if the patient or family asks. The aide tells the patient the request must be reviewed and reports it to the supervising RN the same day.

The supervising RN reviews each request, decides whether the task is within scope and the authorization, and responds to the patient and aide. If the task is appropriate, the RN updates the plan of care and, where needed, asks the plan for a change in authorization.

Aides may not provide supervision or cueing as a standalone service. Aides may not perform nursing tasks, give injections, insert or irrigate catheters, perform sterile procedures, or administer medications. Aides may remind, prompt and assist with self-administration only as described in SVC-08.
Level I authorizations: the Scheduler verifies that scheduled hours do not exceed 8 hours per week, and any request for more goes to the supervising RN and the plan care manager.

The agency does not assign advanced home health aide tasks unless the agency holds the necessary license authority and RN supervision is in place. If a patient needs such a task, an RN performs it or the agency refers the patient to a provider who can.
If a patient refuses an advanced task, the RN documents the refusal and does the task or arranges another provider. The patient suffers no reprisal for refusing (see CR-01).
If the agency proposes any nursing or therapeutic procedure that it has not provided before, the RN Director of Patient Services submits it to the QI Committee before it is offered (see SVC-14).
Aides who are asked to do a task outside their scope, or who are unsure, stop and call the on-call RN or the RN Director of Patient Services before proceeding.

The supervising RN observes aide task performance at supervisory visits (see SVC-07) and documents any task done outside the plan. Task performed outside the plan of care leads to retraining or discipline.
Each aide records the services delivered at every visit, and the record is placed in the clinical record (see REC-01).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the task list, decides scope questions, and approves any new task or service through the QI Committee.
Lists authorized tasks in the plan of care, answers aide questions, and monitors scope at supervisory visits.
Performs only authorized tasks in the plan, declines tasks outside scope, and reports requests to the RN.
Schedules only authorized services and enforces the Level I weekly limit.

documentation: Approved Level I / Level II task list
Plan of care task list by patient
Aide visit records and task sheets
Scope-of-service requests and RN decisions
Documentation of patient refusals of advanced tasks
QI Committee review records for new services

policies.title: Patient Intake, Acceptance Criteria and RN Determination
policies.applies_to: Intake Coordinator, RN Director of Patient Services, admitting and supervising RNs, and administrative staff who receive referrals
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] accepts and keeps only patients whose needs it can safely and adequately meet, and that an RN makes this determination before care begins.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] accepts and retains only patients whose needs can be safely met under written acceptance criteria. Before acceptance, an RN, or a person directly supervised by an RN, determines that the agency can safely and adequately meet the patient's needs. Medicaid personal care patients must have a stable medical condition and be self-directing, unless a responsible person assumes decision-making under the exceptions in the Medicaid rule. They must also meet the minimum needs requirements (see SVC-04). If a referral does not meet them, we decline and refer the patient back to the plan. The rights notice and charge disclosure are documented before the first visit.

definitions.definition: The written conditions the agency uses to decide whether it can accept a referral, including service type, geography, staffing capacity, patient needs and payer authorization.
The documented decision by an RN, or a person directly supervised by an RN, that the agency can safely and adequately meet the patient's needs.
A condition that is not changing so frequently or rapidly that personal care cannot be safely delivered under the plan of care and RN supervision.
Able to make choices about activities of daily living and understand the impact of those choices, or having a responsible person who assumes that role.

procedures: The Administrator and RN Director of Patient Services adopt written acceptance criteria covering counties served, services offered, staffing capacity, language needs, patient needs and payer requirements. The Governing Authority approves them (see GOV-01) and they are reviewed under GOV-03.
The Intake Coordinator logs each referral with the date, source, payer and requested services, and records any referral that is declined and the reason.
For Medicaid or MLTC referrals, the Intake Coordinator confirms that the plan has sent the assessment results, practitioner order and authorization (see SVC-03). Services do not start without them.

The Intake Coordinator checks whether the patient is in a county on the agency license and whether a qualified aide is available for the authorized schedule. If not, the referral is declined promptly and the plan or referral source is told so the patient can be placed elsewhere.

The RN Director of Patient Services, or an RN designee, reviews the referral, the assessment and the order. A person directly supervised by an RN may collect information, but an RN makes or signs the final determination.

The RN confirms the patient is medically stable and self-directing. If the patient cannot self-direct, the RN confirms that a responsible person is willing and able to take on decision-making, and documents who that person is.

The RN confirms the patient meets the minimum needs requirements in SVC-04. If the referral does not meet them, the RN documents the finding, the agency declines to start services and the Intake Coordinator notifies the referring plan the same business day.

The RN reviews the home environment and needs, including safety risks, equipment, sleeping arrangements for live-in cases and any risks to caregivers (see SAF-06), and decides whether the agency can safely meet the patient's needs.
The RN documents the determination, with date, name and title, in the clinical record. The determination states whether the agency accepts the patient, accepts with conditions, or declines.
If the agency declines, the Intake Coordinator informs the patient or referral source in writing, gives the reason, and helps the patient get the referral source to find another provider.

Before the first visit, the Intake Coordinator documents that the patient received the patient rights notice (see CR-01) and the services and charges statement (see CR-06), and that the service agreement is signed.
The RN completes the initial professional assessment and plan of care before or at the start of care (see SVC-06) and assigns an aide whose competencies and language fit the patient's needs.

At each reassessment and plan review, the supervising RN re-confirms that the agency can continue to meet the patient's needs. If it can no longer do so, the RN starts the discharge process in SVC-12.
The Administrator reports acceptance and decline trends and any related complaints to the QI Committee at least quarterly (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures written acceptance criteria exist, are approved and are applied consistently.
Makes or oversees RN determinations and decides whether the agency can safely meet each patient's needs.
Logs referrals, gathers records, checks authorizations and county, and documents rights and charge disclosures.
Completes the determination and the initial assessment, and documents decisions.

documentation: Written acceptance criteria and approval record
Referral log with decline reasons
RN determination of ability to meet needs (date, name, title)
Assessment, practitioner order and plan authorization
Documentation of stability, self-direction and responsible person
Rights notice and charge disclosure acknowledgments
Decline notices to patients and referral sources

policies.title: Medicaid Independent Assessment, Practitioner Order and Reassessment
policies.applies_to: Intake Coordinator, RN Director of Patient Services, supervising RNs, schedulers and care coordination staff
policies.purpose: To make sure Medicaid personal care services begin and continue only on the basis of a valid independent assessment, an independent practitioner order and a current authorization from the plan.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not perform the independent assessment or the independent medical exam for the patients it serves. We rely on the DOH-designated assessment entity, the independent practitioner and the plan. We do not start or continue Medicaid personal care services without a current authorization from the plan. We follow the authorized level, amount, frequency and duration. We support reassessments so that no patient loses services because of a lapse.

definitions.definition: The initial assessment performed by a DOH-designated entity through a NYS-licensed RN with at least two years of recent home health care experience.

definitions.term: Independent medical exam and practitioner order
definitions.definition: An exam and order by a physician, physician assistant, specialist assistant or nurse practitioner who is independent, with no prior provider-patient relationship with the patient.
The Medicaid managed care organization or MLTC plan (or the local district for fee-for-service) that reviews the assessment and order, authorizes services and develops the plan of care.
A later assessment to determine whether the patient's needs and authorization should continue or change. Routine reassessments are annual.

procedures: At referral, the Intake Coordinator asks the plan for the independent assessment results, the independent practitioner order and the written authorization (level, amount, frequency, duration). These are saved in the clinical record.

The Intake Coordinator checks that the assessment was done by the designated assessment entity and that the order is signed and dated by a qualified independent practitioner. If anything is missing or unclear, the Intake Coordinator asks the plan care manager to correct it. Services do not start until the documents are in place.

The RN Director of Patient Services, or an RN designee, reviews the authorization against the assessment and order and the agency's RN determination (see SVC-02). If they do not match, the RN contacts the plan care manager before the first visit.
The agency does not itself act as the independent assessor or independent practitioner, and does not ask a practitioner with a prior treating relationship to serve as the independent examiner.

The plan reviews the assessment and order, authorizes services and develops the plan of care. The agency's RN builds the agency plan of care from that authorization (see SVC-06). Where the plan's record and the agency's record differ, the RN asks the plan to reconcile them.

The plan records the level, amount, frequency and duration of authorized services and sends notice to the enrollee. The Intake Coordinator obtains a copy of the notice or plan authorization and files it.

If assessments are offered by telehealth, the agency does not discourage the patient from choosing an in-person assessment, which must be offered. The agency helps the patient arrange access to the technology or an in-person visit on request.
The Scheduler enters each authorization's start and end dates, and the Intake Coordinator sets a reminder at 90 days and again at 60 days before the authorization expires.
At the 90-day reminder, the Intake Coordinator tells the plan care manager and the patient that a reassessment is due. The agency does not assume that the authorization will be renewed automatically.

Routine reassessments are annual. Authorizations should not run beyond 12 months. If an authorization shows a longer period, the RN Director of Patient Services confirms it with the plan and documents the result.

The agency helps the patient prepare for the reassessment by reminding the patient and family of the appointment, and sharing an RN summary of the patient's needs and any change in condition with the plan, within the limits of CR-03.

If the patient's condition changes significantly between reassessments, the supervising RN notifies the plan care manager and the authorized practitioner promptly and asks for an interim reassessment (see SVC-11).

If a new authorization increases, reduces or ends services, the supervising RN updates the plan of care and the Scheduler updates the schedule only after the written authorization is received. Patients are told of any reduction and of their rights to appeal to the plan (see CR-02).

If an authorization expires without renewal, the Administrator notifies the plan care manager the same business day, and no further services are provided under that authorization unless the plan confirms continued authorization in writing. The RN Director of Patient Services documents the discussion and any referral for safe interim care.
The Administrator reviews a monthly report of authorizations expiring within 90 days and any lapses, and reports lapses to the QI Committee.

responsibilities.duty: Collects the assessment, order and authorization, tracks expiry dates and prompts reassessment requests.
Verifies authorizations match the assessment and order and resolves discrepancies with the plan.
Builds and updates the plan of care to the authorization and requests interim reassessments on change in condition.
Schedules only within current authorizations and halts scheduling on expiry without written renewal.
Monitors authorization lapses and reports to QI.

documentation: Independent assessment results
Independent practitioner order
Plan authorization and enrollee notice (level, amount, frequency, duration)
Authorization tracking log with start and end dates
Communications with the plan about discrepancies and reassessment requests
Plan of care revisions triggered by authorization changes

policies.title: Minimum Needs Requirements and Level I/Level II Authorization Limits
policies.applies_to: Intake Coordinator, RN Director of Patient Services, supervising RNs, schedulers and billing staff
policies.purpose: To make sure the agency applies the Medicaid minimum needs requirements correctly and never schedules or provides services beyond the Level I limits or the plan's authorization.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] accepts Medicaid personal care patients only if they meet the minimum needs requirements. Patients with a diagnosed dementia or Alzheimer's disease must need at least supervision with more than one activity of daily living (ADL). All other patients must need at least limited assistance with physical maneuvering with more than two ADLs. These requirements apply to personal care and consumer directed services applicants age 21 and over, and to Medicaid recipients age 18 and over seeking MLTC or MAP enrollment, at initial assessments and reassessments on or after 9/1/2025. Level I services are limited to 8 hours per week. Care above 12 hours per day on average requires added documentation in the plan. We never schedule beyond the plan's authorization.

definitions.definition: Basic self-care activities such as bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, walking, eating and similar functions, as assessed by the independent assessor.
Hands-on help from another person to complete the activity, as determined in the assessment.
Oversight and prompting needed because of a diagnosed dementia or Alzheimer's disease.

definitions.term: Average of more than 12 hours per day
definitions.definition: Authorization of personal care above 12 hours per day averaged over the authorization period, including continuous and live-in services.

procedures: At referral, the Intake Coordinator confirms the date of the assessment. For assessments or reassessments on or after 9/1/2025, the Intake Coordinator checks that the assessment shows the minimum needs requirements were met.

For patients with a diagnosed dementia or Alzheimer's disease, the RN confirms the diagnosis is documented in the assessment or order and that the assessment shows a need for at least supervision with more than one ADL.
For all other patients, the RN confirms the assessment shows a need for at least limited assistance with physical maneuvering with more than two ADLs.

If the documents do not show the minimum needs requirement is met, the RN does not make the agency the decision maker. The RN documents the finding, the Intake Coordinator tells the plan care manager and refers the patient back to the plan. Services are not started on the strength of the agency's own view of need.
The agency does not change or influence the assessment results. Staff may not coach a patient or family on how to answer assessment questions in order to qualify for services.
The RN lists, in the plan of care, the ADLs on which the patient needs assistance and the level of help for each, so the plan of care is consistent with the assessment (see SVC-06).

The Scheduler checks the authorization for the Level (I or II). For Level I, the Scheduler confirms that scheduled hours do not exceed 8 hours per week and that only Level I tasks are assigned (see SVC-01).

If a Level I patient needs help with personal care functions, the supervising RN tells the plan care manager and requests reassessment for Level II. The aide does not provide Level II tasks until the authorization is changed.

The Scheduler flags any case whose authorized hours average more than 12 hours per day, including continuous and live-in cases. The RN Director of Patient Services confirms that the plan has documented the added information required for that level of care and files a copy.
If the added documentation is missing, the RN Director of Patient Services asks the plan to supply it before services start or continue, and notes the request in the record.

The Scheduler does not schedule hours beyond the authorization. If a patient asks for more hours, or an aide is asked to stay longer, the aide or Scheduler refers the request to the supervising RN, who contacts the care manager about reauthorization.
Billing staff verify that billed hours do not exceed authorized hours and Level. Hours billed above the authorization are reported to the Administrator and not billed to the patient (see CR-06).

The supervising RN reviews at each supervisory visit whether the patient's condition still matches the plan of care and authorization. If the patient's needs have changed, the RN asks the plan care manager for a reassessment.
The Administrator reports minimum-needs declines, Level I limit exceptions and authorization overages to the QI Committee quarterly.

responsibilities.duty: Checks assessment dates and documents, and refers patients who do not meet minimum needs back to the plan.
Verifies minimum needs and added documentation for care above 12 hours per day on average.
Aligns the plan of care to assessed ADL needs and requests reassessment when needs change.
Schedules within the Level, weekly limit and authorized hours, and refers requests for more to the RN.
Bills only authorized hours.

documentation: Assessment showing ADLs and level of need
Diagnosis documentation for dementia or Alzheimer's cases
RN minimum-needs verification note
Referral-back notices to plans
Authorization showing Level and hours; added documentation for above 12 hours per day on average
Reauthorization requests and responses
Schedule and billing reconciliation to authorization

policies.title: Live-in 24-Hour and Continuous Personal Care Services
policies.applies_to: RN Director of Patient Services, supervising RNs, schedulers, payroll staff, live-in aides and continuous-care aides
policies.purpose: To make sure live-in 24-hour and continuous personal care services are provided only to patients who qualify, are staffed correctly, and are paid for in compliance with wage laws.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides live-in 24-hour personal care only when one aide can reasonably be expected to get 5 hours of uninterrupted sleep in an 8-hour sleep period, and continuous personal care only when the patient's needs are frequent enough that this is unlikely. Continuous care means uninterrupted care by more than one aide for more than 16 hours in a calendar day. Both are provided only under a plan authorization and a plan of care. The agency staffs and pays live-in and continuous aides in compliance with federal and State wage law (see PER-06 and PER-11).

definitions.definition: Uninterrupted care by more than one aide for more than 16 hours in a calendar day, for a patient who has a frequent need for toileting, walking, transferring, turning and positioning, or feeding, such that a live-in aide would be unlikely to get 5 hours of uninterrupted sleep.
Care by one aide for a patient whose need for assistance during the night is sufficiently infrequent that the aide is likely to get 5 hours of uninterrupted sleep during an 8-hour period.
The 8-hour period in which the live-in aide is expected to sleep, as set out in the plan of care and schedule.
The State minimum wage for home care aides: $19.65 per hour in NYC, Long Island and Westchester and $18.65 in the rest of the State as of 1/1/2026, rising to $20.00 and $19.00 on 1/1/2027.

procedures: The Intake Coordinator accepts a live-in or continuous referral only with a plan authorization that states the type of service (live-in or continuous), the hours and the duration (see SVC-03).

The RN Director of Patient Services reviews the assessment before acceptance. The RN decides whether the patient's night-time needs fit live-in care or continuous care, based on the frequency of toileting, walking, transferring, turning and positioning, and feeding needs, and documents the reasoning.
If the assessment and authorization do not match the patient's actual night-time needs, the RN asks the plan care manager to review. The agency does not change the service type on its own.

For live-in cases, the RN visits or confirms with the patient and family that the home has sleeping accommodations for the aide, and documents this before the first live-in shift. If there are none, the RN asks the plan for a different arrangement and does not start live-in service.
For live-in cases, the plan of care states the expected sleep period, the aide's daily schedule, and what the patient needs overnight (see SVC-06).
Each live-in aide records in the visit record any night-time interruptions, with the times and the tasks performed. The aide gives the record to the supervising RN each week.

If an aide reports that sleep is regularly interrupted so that 5 hours of uninterrupted sleep is not likely, the supervising RN reviews the record within 3 business days. The RN decides with the care manager whether the patient needs continuous care (more than one aide) and asks the plan for a reassessment.

While the reassessment is pending, the RN Director of Patient Services arranges relief coverage so that the aide is not left without rest, and the patient is safely served. The RN documents what was arranged.

For continuous care, the Scheduler builds a schedule with more than one aide, covers more than 16 hours in the calendar day, and arranges handoff between aides with a written shift report. The Scheduler schedules the same small team where possible (see SVC-09).

Each aide in a continuous case gets a written shift handoff, completed at each change of shift, covering the patient's condition, tasks done and any concerns. The oncoming aide reads it and signs before the outgoing aide leaves.

Cases with authorization averaging more than 12 hours per day require the plan to have supplied the added documentation (see SVC-04). The RN Director of Patient Services files it before services begin.

Payroll staff and the Administrator confirm before the first shift that live-in and continuous aides will be paid at least the home care aide minimum wage ($19.65 NYC, Long Island and Westchester; $18.65 rest of State, as of 1/1/2026; $20.00 and $19.00 from 1/1/2027). They confirm wage parity where it applies and compliance with federal wage law for home care workers, as set out in PER-06 and PER-11.
Payroll staff record the hours the aide works and any sleep and meal breaks according to PER-06, using the electronic visit verification and timekeeping process in SVC-10.

Supervising RNs make supervisory visits at the frequency required in SVC-07, and for live-in and continuous cases they check on aide fatigue, rest, the sleeping area and the safety of the arrangement.
The Administrator reports live-in and continuous cases, sleep interruptions and reassessment requests to the QI Committee quarterly.

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether a patient fits live-in or continuous care, verifies sleeping accommodations and added documentation, and arranges relief coverage.
Reviews sleep-interruption records, asks the plan for reassessment, and supervises these cases.
Builds compliant schedules, arranges shift handoffs, and keeps team continuity.
Ensure pay meets minimum wage, wage parity and wage-law requirements for live-in and continuous aides.
Record interruptions, complete shift handoffs, and report fatigue or safety concerns.

documentation: Plan authorization stating live-in or continuous type, hours and duration
RN service-type determination with reasoning
Confirmation of sleeping accommodations (live-in)
Aide night-time interruption records
Reassessment requests and plan responses
Shift handoff reports (continuous)
Wage and timekeeping records showing minimum wage and wage parity compliance

policies.title: Plan of Care and Plan Updates
policies.applies_to: RN Director of Patient Services, Supervising RNs, intake and scheduling staff, and all personal care aides
policies.purpose: To make sure every patient has a written plan of care built on a professional assessment, that the plan is reviewed and revised on schedule, and that patients, aides, practitioners and payers are told about changes.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will not provide services without a written plan of care built on a professional assessment by a registered nurse. The plan covers diagnosis, prognosis, mental status, the frequency of each service, medications, treatments, diet regimens, functional limitations and rehabilitation potential (10 NYCRR §766.3). The agency reviews and revises each plan as often as the patient's condition requires, and at least every six months, and documents every review in the clinical record. The patient takes part in planning and is told in advance of changes. Significant changes in condition are promptly reported to the authorized practitioner and other affected providers. Plan changes are reported to the payer that authorized the services (10 NYCRR §766.5(b)). For Medicaid patients, the agency's plan of care works within the assessment and authorization made by the local district or the MLTC plan (MMCO). It does not replace them and does not exceed authorized hours or tasks.

definitions.definition: The written document, based on a professional assessment, that states what services the patient will receive, how often and by whom, along with the clinical elements required by 10 NYCRR §766.3.
An assessment of the patient's needs, home and supports made by a registered nurse licensed in New York State.
The physician or other qualified practitioner who orders the patient's services.
The entity that authorizes and pays for services, such as the local social services district, an MLTC plan or a private-pay client.
A change in the patient's health, function, mental status, medications, safety or home situation that may require the plan, services or hours to change.

procedures: Before the first visit, the RN reviews the practitioner's order, the Medicaid independent assessment or payer authorization (if any), and any plan the district or MLTC plan has sent. The RN notes the authorized tasks, hours and duration.

The RN completes the agency's professional assessment in the home, with the patient and, if the patient wishes, a family member or representative. The RN does this before services start, or at the first visit if the patient needs urgent services.

The RN writes the plan of care, which includes: diagnosis; prognosis; mental status; the frequency of each service; medications; treatments; diet regimen; functional limitations; and rehabilitation potential.

The RN lists on the plan the specific tasks the aide may perform, tied to the authorized level of service, and the observations and reports the aide must make. The RN also states any safety precautions.
The RN states on the plan the frequency of RN supervisory visits that applies to the patient, as set by the payer or the MLTC contract (see SVC-07).

The RN reviews the plan with the patient or representative, explains it in language the patient understands, and records the patient's input and preferences. Patients are told before the plan is changed. The RN documents this discussion.

Within [NUMBER OF DAYS, e.g., 2] business days of completing the plan, the RN files it in the clinical record, gives the patient a copy of the services and schedule, and makes the plan available to the assigned aide before the aide's first visit.
The Supervising RN instructs the aide on the plan at or before the first visit, and records that the aide reviewed it. The aide may only perform tasks on the plan.

The Supervising RN reviews the plan at every supervisory visit and whenever the patient's needs, hours or authorization change. Each review gets a dated, signed entry in the record, even if no revision is needed.

The scheduling coordinator tracks each plan's six-month review date. The system flags each plan 30 days before its date. The RN Director of Patient Services reviews a monthly overdue-review report, and no plan may go more than six months without a documented review.

When the patient's condition changes significantly, the RN promptly notifies the authorized practitioner and other affected providers (SVC-11), revises the plan, and documents the notice and the practitioner's response.

When a plan revision affects authorized hours, tasks or service frequency, the RN notifies the payer or care manager within [NUMBER, e.g., 2] business days, in writing, and documents it. The agency does not change authorized hours without payer approval.
The RN tells the patient and the aide about any revision before it takes effect, except in an emergency. The RN documents who was told, when and how.
A revised plan replaces the earlier plan in the record. The earlier version is kept and marked superseded.

The RN Director of Patient Services audits a sample of plans each quarter for required elements, six-month reviews, patient participation and payer notification, and reports the results to the QI Committee (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Completes the assessment, writes and revises the plan, involves the patient, instructs the aide, notifies the practitioner and payer, and documents each review.
Ensures plans meet regulatory elements, reviews overdue-review reports and audits plans quarterly.
Tracks review dates, flags upcoming reviews and makes sure aides' schedules match the plan.
Works only within the plan, reports observations and changes to the Supervising RN.
Takes part in planning and tells the agency about changes in needs.

documentation: Signed and dated professional assessment
Plan of care in the clinical record with all required elements
Dated six-month and interim plan review entries
Record of patient participation and advance notice of changes
Notices to the practitioner, other providers and payer about plan changes
Aide's acknowledgment of plan instruction
Overdue-review tracking report and quarterly audit results

policies.title: Supervision of Aides and RN Supervisory Visits
policies.applies_to: RN Director of Patient Services, Supervising RNs, scheduling staff and all personal care aides
policies.purpose: To make sure personal care aides are supervised by a registered nurse, that RN visits in the home happen on time, and that every visit is documented in a way that supports patient safety and payment.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] employs enough trained supervisory staff to supervise all aides (10 NYCRR §766.5). Aides are supervised as appropriate by a registered nurse. Only an RN makes supervisory visits, and the aide is present for the visit so the RN can observe care and give instruction. In-home supervision takes place (1) at the initial service visit, or when the aide changes, if the aide lacks documented training and experience in the tasks, with return demonstration; (2) when the patient's condition changes, to evaluate and revise the plan; and (3) to instruct the aide on required observations and written reports. For Medicaid patients, the agency's default is an RN supervisory visit at least every 90 days. The frequency is stated on each plan of care and confirmed against each MLTC plan or district contract, because later DOH rulemaking leaves frequency to the district or MMCO and some counties accept a six-month visit for stable, self-directing clients. The agency applies a shorter interval whenever the contract, the plan or the patient's condition calls for one. A written report is made for each supervisory visit and filed in the clinical record. Every aide also receives an annual performance assessment that includes at least one in-home observation (10 NYCRR §766.11).

definitions.definition: An in-home visit by a registered nurse, with the aide present, to observe the aide's care, evaluate the patient and the plan, and instruct the aide.
The aide performs a task while the RN watches to confirm the aide can do it correctly and safely.
A Medicaid managed care organization, including an MLTC plan, that authorizes and pays for services.
The interval at which an RN must visit, as set on the plan of care or by the contract with the payer, and never longer than the payer allows.

procedures: At acceptance, the RN Director of Patient Services or Supervising RN identifies the payer and checks the contract or district instructions for the required supervisory visit frequency. If the source is unclear, the RN confirms it in writing with the plan or district and keeps the answer in the record.
The RN writes the supervisory visit frequency on the plan of care (SVC-06). If no payer rule is found, the agency uses a visit at least every 90 days.

If a combined visit every six months is allowed for a stable, self-directing client, the RN documents the payer's written permission and the client's stability in the record. Otherwise the 90-day schedule applies.

At the initial visit, or when an aide new to the patient starts, the RN decides whether the aide has documented training and experience in the tasks on the plan. If not, the RN goes to the home, observes the aide and requires return demonstration of each task.

The RN records the result of the return demonstration. If the aide cannot perform a task safely, the RN gives further instruction and does not allow the aide to perform it alone until competence is documented.

The scheduling coordinator enters each patient's next due date in the tracking system. The system flags visits due within 14 days. The coordinator assigns a Supervising RN and books the visit when the aide is on duty.

Each supervisory visit is made with the aide present. The RN observes care, checks the patient's condition, home safety and informal supports, reviews the aide's activity sheets and observations, and asks the patient about satisfaction.
The RN instructs the aide on required observations and what to report, and gives written reporting instructions that the aide acknowledges.

The RN writes a report for each visit on the day of the visit or no later than [NUMBER, e.g., 2] business days after. The report names the aide, the patient, the date and the findings. It also records any instruction given, any change needed to the plan and the next due date. The RN signs and files it in the record.
If the patient's condition changes, or the aide reports a problem, the RN makes an in-home visit promptly to evaluate and revise the plan (SVC-11).
If a visit cannot be done on time because the patient is unavailable or refuses, the RN documents each attempt, notifies the payer or care manager and reschedules within [NUMBER, e.g., 7] days.

The RN Director of Patient Services reviews a weekly report of overdue and upcoming visits. Any visit that is overdue goes to the Director the same day. OMIG audit guidance describes disallowance of claims where no documented RN visit occurred within 120 days before the date of service. The agency treats 120 days as a hard internal limit and does not rely on it as the standard.

The RN Director of Patient Services holds billing for any patient whose supervisory visit documentation is missing until it is corrected or the visit is made, and consults the Compliance Officer on any claim already submitted (GOV-05).
Each aide receives an annual performance assessment that includes at least one in-home observation by an RN. The RN documents the observation in the personnel record (PER-10).

The RN Director of Patient Services reviews supervisory visit timeliness and report completeness each quarter and reports results to the QI Committee (GOV-04). The Director also confirms staffing is sufficient for the supervisory workload.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures enough RNs, confirms frequency rules for each payer, reviews overdue reports and holds billing when documentation is missing.
Makes supervisory visits with the aide present, completes return demonstrations, instructs aides and files a report for every visit.
Tracks due dates, books visits and flags overdue visits.
Is present for supervisory visits, follows instruction and reports observations.
Reviews any claim lacking required supervisory documentation.

documentation: Supervisory visit frequency on the plan of care and the payer source for it
Written report for each supervisory visit, signed and dated by the RN
Return demonstration records
Aide acknowledgment of reporting instructions
Attempts to schedule and reschedule missed visits
Overdue and upcoming visit tracking reports
Annual in-home observation record in the personnel file
Quarterly QI summary of supervisory visit timeliness

policies.title: Medication Assistance and Self-Administration Support
policies.applies_to: Personal care aides, Supervising RNs and the RN Director of Patient Services
policies.purpose: To define the limited help with medications that personal care aides may give and to prohibit medication administration.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] personal care aides may support a patient's own administration of medication. Under 18 NYCRR §505.14(a)(5)(ii), Level II personal care covers medication prompting and assistance but not administration. Aides may: prompt the patient as to time; identify the medication; bring the medication and supplies; open the container; position the patient; dispose of used supplies; and store the medication properly. Aides do not administer medication, which means they do not put medication into the patient's body, measure or draw up doses, inject, or decide what or how much the patient takes. Medication administration by an advanced home health aide requires an RN comprehensive medication review and direct RN supervision under 10 NYCRR §766.5(e). The agency does not provide advanced home health aide services, so this policy does not cover them. If the agency adds AHHA services, a new policy must first go through QI Committee review (SVC-14). The aide reports medication problems to the supervising RN and records them in observation notes.

definitions.definition: Reminding the patient that it is time to take a medication the patient takes on his or her own.
The patient takes or applies his or her own medication, with the aide limited to the supporting tasks listed in this policy.
Giving a medication to a patient or putting it into the patient's body, including measuring doses, injecting, placing in the mouth or applying treatment. Aides do not do this.
A missed dose, refusal, wrong or unlabeled medication, apparent side effect, confusion about a medication, an expired or missing supply, or any other medication concern.

procedures: At assessment, the RN reviews the patient's medication list and the ability of the patient to take the medication independently. The RN records the medications, who sets them up and any assistance needed.

If the patient cannot take medication unaided, even with prompting, the RN does not assign medication tasks to the aide. The RN contacts the authorized practitioner and the care manager about other arrangements, such as a family member, a nurse visit or pharmacy packaging.
The RN lists on the plan of care only the medication support tasks the aide may perform for that patient, taken from the permitted list in this policy, and writes any precautions.

At the first visit or before the aide starts, the RN instructs the aide in the permitted tasks and the limits, and the aide signs that he or she understands the tasks. The aide must give the RN return demonstration if the aide has no documented training in the tasks.

When assisting, the aide confirms the label and identifies the medication as the patient's. The aide prompts the patient at the time stated on the label or plan, brings the supplies, opens the container and positions the patient. The patient takes the medication.
The aide never measures, pours or selects a dose, crushes tablets, gives injections or breaks tablets unless the patient does it. The aide never gives a patient another person's medication.
The aide disposes of used supplies and stores the medication in the proper place, for example in the refrigerator if the label says so.

If the patient refuses a medication, the aide does not force or persuade the patient beyond a reminder. The aide records the refusal and calls the Supervising RN the same day. If a patient has a serious reaction or a medication emergency, the aide follows SVC-11.
The aide reports to the Supervising RN any medication problem the same day (or immediately if it is urgent), and records it in the observation notes for the visit.
The RN evaluates the report, contacts the authorized practitioner or pharmacy if needed, revises the plan if the patient's ability has changed and documents the action in the record.

If an aide gives a medication, or helps in a way outside this policy, the aide reports it at once to the RN. The RN assesses the patient, notifies the practitioner and files an incident report (SAF-02).
At each supervisory visit, the RN reviews the aide's medication notes with the patient and the aide, and confirms the aide is working within the permitted tasks (SVC-07).
The RN Director of Patient Services reviews medication-related reports and incidents quarterly and presents trends to the QI Committee (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Assesses ability for self-administration, lists permitted tasks, instructs the aide, evaluates medication problems and notifies the practitioner.
Performs only permitted support tasks, never administers medication, and reports problems the same day.
Enforces the limits, reviews incidents and reports trends to the QI Committee.
Takes the medication and tells the agency about changes in medications.

documentation: Medication list and self-administration assessment in the clinical record
Plan of care listing permitted medication support tasks
Aide instruction record and return demonstration
Aide observation notes describing medication problems
RN follow-up entries and practitioner contacts
Incident reports for any medication event
Quarterly review summary

policies.title: Scheduling, Missed Visits and Continuity of Care
policies.applies_to: Scheduling staff, Supervising RNs, personal care aides and the RN Director of Patient Services
policies.purpose: To make sure services are delivered at the times and frequencies in the plan of care, by consistent and qualified aides, with documented backup coverage when a visit is missed.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] delivers services at the times and frequencies in each plan of care. To the extent possible, the same aides serve the same patient (10 NYCRR §766.2). Staff are assigned according to licensure, training, orientation and demonstrated skills (10 NYCRR §766.5). Every missed or late visit is documented, backup or make-up coverage is arranged, and the plan or care manager is notified when authorized hours are not delivered. The agency's written emergency plan keeps patients' health needs met during disruptions, and the agency maintains 24/7 emergency contacts (10 NYCRR §766.9).

definitions.definition: A scheduled visit that does not take place, or that is shorter than scheduled, for any reason.
A visit that starts more than [15] minutes after the scheduled start time.
A qualified substitute aide, assigned by the agency, who covers a visit the regular aide cannot make.
The practice of assigning the same aide or a small team of aides to a patient so the patient's care is consistent.

procedures: When a patient is accepted, the scheduling coordinator builds the schedule from the plan of care, matching days, times and hours to the plan and the authorization. The schedule may not exceed authorized hours.

The coordinator assigns a primary aide and, where possible, a named backup aide. The assignment considers the aide's training, orientation, demonstrated skills, language and the patient's needs, as confirmed by the Supervising RN.
The coordinator gives the patient the aide's name and the agency's phone number, [PHONE], and tells the patient how to report a late or missed visit.

An aide who cannot work a scheduled visit must call the agency at [PHONE] as early as possible, and at least [NUMBER, e.g., 4] hours before the visit unless it is an emergency. An aide who is running more than [15] minutes late must call the coordinator.

The coordinator tries to find a qualified backup aide immediately, starting with the named backup. The coordinator tells the patient who is coming and when. If a new aide is sent, the coordinator tells the Supervising RN, who decides whether an in-home visit is needed under SVC-07.

If the patient is high-risk, for example has dementia, lives alone or has a time-critical need, the coordinator tells the Supervising RN at once if no backup can be found. The RN decides on other arrangements, including a nurse visit or contacting family or the care manager.

If a visit is missed and no backup is found, the coordinator calls the patient the same day, explains the situation, offers a make-up visit within the authorization where permitted, and records the call.
If a patient is not home, does not answer the door or refuses entry, the aide calls the coordinator. If the patient is at risk, the Supervising RN follows SVC-11 and may request a welfare check.
The coordinator records each missed or late visit in the missed visit log with the date, patient, aide, reason, backup action and whether a make-up visit was done.

When authorized hours are not delivered, the coordinator or RN notifies the MLTC plan, district or care manager by the next business day, or sooner if the patient is at risk. The agency tells the payer which hours were missed, why and how they will be made up.

The RN Director of Patient Services reviews the missed visit log weekly. The Director investigates repeated missed visits by the same aide or to the same patient, and takes corrective action with the aide, the schedule or the staffing level.
When a regular aide leaves, takes leave or is reassigned, the coordinator tells the patient in advance if possible, introduces the new aide and schedules RN instruction if needed.

The agency keeps a written on-call rotation so that a coordinator and an RN can be reached 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Evening and weekend contact information is given to every patient and aide.
During a disruption such as severe weather or a staffing emergency, the agency follows its emergency plan (SAF-05). It prioritizes patients by risk and keeps patients' health needs met.
The RN Director of Patient Services reports missed-visit rates, backup coverage success and continuity (the share of visits by the primary aide) to the QI Committee quarterly (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Builds schedules to the plan, assigns aides, arranges backup, logs missed visits and notifies patients and payers.
Confirms assignments match skills, decides on alternatives for high-risk patients and evaluates new-aide needs.
Arrives on time, calls early if unable to work and reports access problems.
Reviews the missed visit log, investigates patterns and reports to the QI Committee.
Maintains sufficient staff and 24/7 contacts.

documentation: Patient schedule and aide assignment records
Missed and late visit log
Records of calls to patients and backup arrangements
Notices to payers or care managers about undelivered hours
On-call rotation and 24/7 contact lists
Weekly review notes and corrective actions
Quarterly QI report on missed visits and continuity

policies.title: Electronic Visit Verification and Timekeeping
policies.applies_to: Personal care aides, scheduling and billing staff, payroll staff and the Compliance Officer
policies.purpose: To make sure every Medicaid personal care visit is verified electronically, that time and payment records are accurate and complete, and that EVV data matches authorizations before billing.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] uses electronic visit verification for all Medicaid personal care services, as required since January 1, 2021 under the 21st Century Cures Act (42 USC 1396b(l)). New York uses a choice model, and the agency has selected [EVV VENDOR] as its EVV system. The system sends visit data to the NYS EVV Data Aggregator and captures the date of service, location, type of service, the individuals involved and the start and end times. The agency keeps time and payment records for all personnel (10 NYCRR §766.11), and keeps the records required by federal wage and hour law (29 CFR 516 and 552). EVV data is reconciled against authorizations before any claim is submitted.

definitions.definition: Electronic visit verification: an electronic system that records the date, location, service, people and start and end times of a visit.
The New York State system that receives EVV data from agencies' EVV vendors.
The New York approach under which each agency picks its own EVV vendor, so long as it sends data to the Data Aggregator.
A visit with missing, late, manually edited or inconsistent EVV data, such as a missing clock-in, location mismatch or hours that differ from the schedule.
A change to EVV time or location data made by someone other than the aide at the time of the visit.

procedures: The Administrator selects and contracts with the EVV vendor, confirms that it can send required data elements to the NYS EVV Data Aggregator, and documents the confirmation. The Administrator reviews the vendor annually.

At hire and before the first visit, the coordinator trains each aide on the EVV system, including how to start and end each visit, what to do if the device does not work and the prohibition on falsifying data. The aide signs an acknowledgment, which goes in the personnel file.
For each visit, the aide starts the visit in the EVV system on arrival at the patient's home and ends it when care is finished. Times must reflect actual start and end, not scheduled times.
The aide never clocks in or out for another person, never clocks in away from the home unless authorized (for example, an errand or escort in SAF-08), and never asks a patient to enter visit data.

If the device fails or the aide cannot use EVV, the aide calls the agency immediately at [PHONE]. The coordinator records the reason and the aide's actual times, and enters a manual entry using the procedure below.

A manual edit may be made only by the coordinator with a documented reason code, the name of the person who made the edit and the date. The aide must confirm the corrected times. Edits are not made to meet a schedule or authorized total.
The billing specialist reviews EVV exceptions daily and records them in the EVV exceptions log with the visit, cause, resolution and who resolved it.

Before each billing cycle, the billing specialist reconciles EVV visits to the authorization (service, hours, dates) and to the plan of care, and corrects or holds claims that do not match. Claims are never submitted for visits not verified or not authorized.

Payroll staff pay aides from verified time records. Payroll records show hours worked, wages, deductions and dates, and meet 29 CFR 516 and 552, including time spent on live-in schedules where applicable (PER-06).

The Compliance Officer reviews a random sample of visits each month, comparing EVV records, aide activity sheets, schedules and payroll. The Officer investigates any pattern of manual edits, round-number times or location mismatches, and follows GOV-05 if there is suspected fraud.

Time and payment records and patient-care financial records are kept at least three years, and personnel records at least three years after separation. The EVV system keeps data securely and confidentially, and the agency can print it on request (10 NYCRR §766.12).
The agency follows the EVV vendor's and DOH's data security requirements, and EVV data is protected as patient information under CR-03.
