The Compliance Officer reports EVV exception rates, manual edit rates and reconciliation findings to the QI Committee at least quarterly (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Records actual start and end of each visit and reports device problems at once.
Trains aides on EVV, resolves failures and makes documented manual edits only.
Reviews exceptions daily, reconciles EVV to authorizations before billing and holds unmatched claims.
Pays from verified time and keeps wage and hour records.
Audits samples monthly, investigates patterns and reports to the QI Committee.
Selects and monitors the EVV vendor and ensures data goes to the Data Aggregator.

documentation: EVV vendor contract and confirmation of Data Aggregator connection
Aide EVV training acknowledgments
EVV visit data showing date, location, service, people and start and end times
EVV exceptions log and manual edit records with reason codes
Billing reconciliation worksheets
Time and payroll records
Monthly compliance audit reports
Quarterly QI report on EVV

policies.title: Change in Client Condition and Emergencies in the Home
policies.applies_to: Personal care aides, Supervising RNs, scheduling staff and the RN Director of Patient Services
policies.purpose: To make sure aides recognize and report changes in a patient's condition and emergencies, that an RN evaluates and acts, and that practitioners, payers and families are notified promptly.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires prompt charting and reporting of changes in condition, adverse reactions and problems with informal supports or the home (10 NYCRR §766.5(b)). An RN evaluates the patient in the home when the condition changes and initiates revision of the plan of care (10 NYCRR §766.5(d)). Staff promptly alert the authorized practitioner and other affected providers to significant changes in condition (10 NYCRR §766.3(d)). Accidents and incidents are documented in the clinical record (10 NYCRR §766.6(a)). As agency procedure, aides call 911 for any life-threatening emergency and then notify the supervising RN. Aides do not diagnose, treat or decide whether a patient needs medical care.

definitions.definition: Any new or worsening physical, mental, behavioral or functional change in a patient, any adverse reaction to a medication or treatment, or a problem with the home or informal supports that could affect safety or care.

A situation that may cause death or serious harm without immediate help, such as unresponsiveness, trouble breathing, chest pain, stroke signs, severe bleeding, serious fall with injury, choking or a fire.
Family, friends and neighbors who help care for the patient without pay.
The practitioner who ordered the patient's services.

procedures: At the first visit and at each supervisory visit, the RN teaches the aide the signs of a change in condition for that patient (for example, new confusion, falls, skin changes, poor intake, pain, shortness of breath, medication problems or unsafe conditions in the home) and the reporting steps in this policy.

In a life-threatening emergency, the aide calls 911 first, stays with the patient and gives first aid only within the aide's training. The aide does not move an injured person unless there is immediate danger.

After calling 911, the aide immediately calls the agency at [PHONE], where the coordinator or on-call RN is reached at all hours. The aide gives the patient's name, what happened and what has been done.

The coordinator or on-call RN notifies the Supervising RN at once, if that person is not already on the call, and the RN notifies the patient's representative or emergency contact. The aide may do so if the RN directs it.

For a change in condition that is not an emergency, the aide calls the Supervising RN or agency office the same day, before leaving the home if the patient appears at risk, and gives the specific observations.
The aide writes down the change in the observation notes for the visit the same day, using objective facts, times and what the patient said, and gives it to the supervisor as the agency directs.
The Supervising RN assesses the report immediately, by phone if appropriate, and decides if the patient needs emergency care, practitioner contact or an RN visit. The RN documents the decision.

The RN makes an in-home visit to evaluate the patient when the condition has changed, within [24] hours or sooner if the risk requires. The RN evaluates the patient, home and supports, and instructs the aide as needed.

The RN promptly alerts the authorized practitioner and other affected providers to any significant change, and records the date, time, who was told, what was said and any orders. If the practitioner cannot be reached, the RN escalates according to agency practice and documents each attempt.

The RN revises the plan of care if needed, tells the patient and aide, and notifies the payer or care manager of changes in services or hours (SVC-06). If the change calls for more services than authorized, the RN contacts the payer about a reassessment (SVC-03).
If the aide cannot get into the home, finds the patient not responding, or the patient is missing, the aide calls the agency. The RN or coordinator arranges a welfare check or calls 911 as needed.

For problems with informal supports or the home, such as no heat, unsafe wiring, pests, absent caregivers or neglect, the aide reports to the RN, who documents it, tries to resolve it with the patient and family, and reports to the payer or appropriate authority where required (SAF-01).

For any accident or incident, including a fall, injury, medication event or emergency response, the RN completes an incident report on the day of the event and files it with the clinical record (SAF-02).

After any emergency, the RN follows up with the patient or family within [24] hours of hospitalization or return home, and records the outcome. If the patient is hospitalized, the RN follows SVC-12 for any hold or resumption of services.

The RN Director of Patient Services reviews all emergencies and significant changes in condition monthly, assesses whether reporting and response were timely, and reports trends to the QI Committee (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Calls 911 in life-threatening emergencies, reports changes the same day and records observations.
Evaluates in the home, alerts the practitioner and other providers, revises the plan and notifies payers and family.
Answers calls at all hours, notifies the Supervising RN and arranges welfare checks.
Reviews events monthly, ensures timeliness and reports trends.
Ensures 24/7 coverage and resources for response.

documentation: Aide observation notes describing the change or emergency
RN assessment and in-home evaluation notes
Record of notice to the authorized practitioner and other providers, with date, time and response
Revised plan of care and notice to payer or care manager
Incident report and follow-up notes
Notices to family or representative
Monthly review and QI trend report

policies.title: Discharge, Transfer and Discontinuation of Services
policies.applies_to: All patients, the RN Director of Patient Services, supervising RNs, scheduling and intake staff, and personal care aides
policies.purpose: To make sure that no patient's services end, transfer or are discontinued without a planned, safe and documented process. The process must meet the New York State Department of Health requirements for discharge planning, practitioner notice, patient consultation and the discharge summary.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] starts a discharge plan before any discharge, transfer or discontinuation of services (10 NYCRR §766.2(a)(8)). The agency discharges a patient only after it has notified the authorized practitioner and consulted the patient and the professional staff involved in the plan of care. This happens at least 48 hours before the discharge (10 NYCRR §766.2(a)(9)). A discharge summary is completed and placed in the patient care record (10 NYCRR §766.6(a)(10)). For members of a Managed Long Term Care (MLTC) plan, the plan holds the authorization and member-notice responsibilities. The agency coordinates with the plan and does not issue plan notices on its behalf (42 CFR 438.404). The agency does not abandon a patient. Where the agency itself ends services, it makes sure the patient has a safe transition or referral.

definitions.definition: The planned end of all services by the agency to a patient, whether the reason is goals met, no longer needing services, patient request, transfer to another agency or program, or agency-initiated discontinuation.
Movement of a patient's care to another home care agency, program, facility or payer arrangement, with the agency's records and information shared as permitted.
The physician, nurse practitioner or other practitioner who ordered the patient's services and is authorized to order them.
The record entry that documents discharge planning, notice to the practitioner, reasons and date, summary of care, status at discharge, remaining needs, ability to self-manage, and referrals.
The Medicaid managed long term care plan that authorizes services for an enrolled member and is responsible for member notices about changes in authorized services.

procedures: Any staff member who learns that a patient may stop services (patient or family request, move, hospital or facility admission, loss of coverage, safety concern, or end of authorization) notifies the RN Director of Patient Services the same business day.

The RN Director of Patient Services, or a designated supervising RN, opens a discharge plan in the patient care record before the discharge date. The plan records the reason, the proposed date, the patient's remaining needs and the proposed referrals.

The supervising RN identifies the payer. If the patient is an MLTC member, the RN contacts the plan's care manager before any notice is given to the patient. The RN confirms who will send required member notices, whether the plan is changing or ending authorization, and what transition steps the plan will arrange (see SVC-13).

The supervising RN consults the patient, or the patient's legally authorized representative, about the proposed discharge. The RN explains the reason, the date and the options for continued care. The RN documents the consultation in a signed and dated progress note.

The supervising RN consults the professional staff involved in the plan of care (the assigned aide, the aide's supervisor and any other RN or professional involved). The RN documents the consultation.
The supervising RN notifies the authorized practitioner of the planned discharge. Notice is given by phone, fax or secure message, and the RN documents the date, time, method and person notified.

The agency completes the practitioner notification and the patient and staff consultation at least 48 hours before the discharge. No discharge date is set that does not allow for this. The agency gives as much additional advance notice as is practicable and safe.

If the discharge is unplanned and a 48-hour notice is impossible (for example the patient dies, is admitted to a hospital, or moves without notice), the RN Director of Patient Services notifies the practitioner as soon as the agency learns of the event. The RN Director documents why advance notice was not possible.

If the agency itself must discontinue services (for example an unsafe home environment that cannot be corrected, or the needs of the patient can no longer be met under the agency's acceptance criteria), the RN Director of Patient Services reviews the case before any decision is made. The RN Director documents the reasons and the steps taken to resolve the problem first (see SVC-02 and SAF-06).

For an agency-initiated discontinuation, the agency gives the patient written notice stating the reason and date, who to contact, and how to file a complaint or appeal (see CR-02). The agency continues services until the discharge date unless staff safety or patient safety requires an earlier stop. If services are stopped earlier for safety, the RN Director of Patient Services documents the reason.

The supervising RN arranges referrals and transition for the patient. These may include another licensed home care agency, the MLTC plan care manager, the local social services district, adult day services, or community resources. The RN gives the patient the contact information in writing.
With the patient's consent, or as otherwise permitted by law (see CR-03), the agency shares the necessary care information with the receiving agency, facility or care manager.

The supervising RN completes the discharge summary at or before the discharge date. The summary records the discharge planning, notice to the practitioner, reasons and date, a summary of care provided, the patient's status at discharge, remaining needs, ability to self-manage, and referrals made.
Scheduling staff end all visits as of the discharge date, remove the patient from the schedule and the EVV system (see SVC-10), and notify the assigned aides.
The agency recovers any agency property from the home or patient (for example agency forms) and confirms that the aide has no remaining patient property or keys (see CR-04).

The RN Director of Patient Services reviews all discharge cases at the next QI Committee meeting as part of the sample of discharges reviewed (see GOV-04). The Committee also reviews any complaints connected to a discharge.
The Health Information Manager closes the record and stores it under the retention rules in REC-01.

responsibilities.duty: Oversees all discharge planning, approves agency-initiated discontinuations, makes sure the 48-hour practitioner notice and consultation requirements are met, and reviews discharge summaries for completeness.
Develops the discharge plan, consults the patient and staff, notifies the practitioner, coordinates with the MLTC plan, arranges referrals and completes the discharge summary.
Notify the RN of any patient-reported intent to stop services, remove discharged patients from schedules and EVV, and inform assigned aides.
Reports to the supervising RN any patient or family comments about stopping services or any changes in the home, and participates in consultation about the plan of care.
Makes sure the agency has the resources to carry out safe discharges and reviews any complaint or appeal relating to a discharge.

documentation: Discharge plan opened before the date of discharge
Dated note of the consultation with the patient or authorized representative
Dated note of the consultation with professional staff involved in the plan of care
Record of notice to the authorized practitioner, including date, time, method and person notified
Record of coordination with the MLTC plan care manager and any plan notices
Written notice to the patient for an agency-initiated discontinuation
Referral and transition information given to the patient
Discharge summary meeting the content required by 10 NYCRR §766.6(a)(10)

policies.title: Coordination with Medicaid Programs, MLTC Plans and Payers
policies.applies_to: Intake and billing staff, the RN Director of Patient Services, supervising RNs, the Administrator, and any staff who communicate with the local district, MLTC plans or other payers
policies.purpose: To make sure that [AGENCY NAME] delivers only the Medicaid personal care that has been authorized, records and follows the authorization, contracts properly with MLTC plans, and refers patients to the right Medicaid programs when their needs or preferences call for something other than the agency's services.
policies.policy: Medicaid personal care services are authorized by the local social services district or the Medicaid managed care organization (MMCO), including an MLTC plan. Services must be medically necessary, ordered by a qualified independent practitioner, based on assessment, delivered under a plan of care and supervised by a registered nurse (18 NYCRR 505.14(a)(1)). The agency delivers services only at the level, amount, frequency and duration that the district or plan has authorized. The plan must record the level, amount, frequency and duration in the plan of care and give notice to the enrollee (18 NYCRR 505.14(b)(2)(iii); DOH Medicaid Managed Care NYIA guidance). The agency tracks the Minimum Needs Requirements that apply to initial assessments and reassessments on or after 9/1/2025 (see SVC-04). Before the agency enters an MLTC contract, it gets the rate, billing codes and units, authorization process and wage pass-through terms in writing. The agency does not operate as a Consumer Directed Personal Assistance Program (CDPAP) fiscal intermediary. It refers patients who want CDPAP to the plan or care manager.

definitions.definition: A Medicaid managed care organization, including a managed long term care (MLTC) plan, that authorizes and pays for services for its enrolled members.
The local social services district responsible for authorizing Medicaid personal care for people who are not enrolled in a managed care plan.
The elements of the authorization that state the level of personal care (Level I or Level II), the hours, the schedule and the length of time authorized.
The New York Independent Assessor, the entity that conducts the independent assessment and arranges the independent practitioner order on which Medicaid authorization depends.
The Consumer Directed Personal Assistance Program. Public Partnerships LLC (PPL) is the single Statewide Fiscal Intermediary, and LHCSAs no longer serve as CDPAP fiscal intermediaries.
A contract term requiring that a stated part of the rate paid to the agency be used for aide wages or benefits.

procedures: At referral, Intake Staff record the patient's payer (local district, MLTC plan, other Medicaid managed care, private pay or other) and the name and phone number of the care manager or district contact.

Before accepting a Medicaid patient, Intake Staff obtain a copy of the authorization or plan of care showing the level, amount, frequency and duration of services, and the start date. The staff member refers the file to the RN Director of Patient Services for review under SVC-02.

The RN Director of Patient Services confirms that the authorization is consistent with the independent assessment and practitioner order (see SVC-03). Where a Level I or Level II limit or the Minimum Needs Requirements apply, the RN confirms how the authorization addresses them (see SVC-04). Any inconsistency is raised with the plan or district before services begin.

The agency schedules and delivers only the authorized services. A supervising RN reconciles the patient's plan of care (see SVC-06) with the authorization at start of care and each time the authorization changes.

If the supervising RN believes the patient needs more or less service than authorized, the RN documents the observed need and sends a written request to the plan care manager or district. The agency does not change hours on its own.
At least once each month, Billing Staff compare authorized hours with hours delivered, using the EVV records (see SVC-10). They report differences to the RN Director of Patient Services.

When the agency learns that an MLTC member's authorization has been reduced, suspended or ended, the supervising RN contacts the plan care manager the same business day to confirm the date and the plan's notice to the member. The agency does not issue the plan's notice (see SVC-12).
When reassessments are due, the supervising RN contacts the plan or district in advance, shares relevant records as permitted (see CR-03), and informs the patient about the process.

Before signing any MLTC contract, the Administrator confirms that the plan has capacity to contract under DOH's contract limits. Plans may contract with no more than one LHCSA per 100 enrollees downstate or per 60 rest of state, with at least two LHCSAs per county accepting new enrollees. Contract-limit exceptions are requested from LHCSAExceptions@health.ny.gov.

Before signing, the Administrator obtains in the written contract the rate, the billing codes and units, the authorization process, claims and payment timelines, and any wage pass-through requirement. Legal counsel reviews the contract. The contract is filed with the agency's records (see REC-03 and GOV-06).

The Administrator keeps a contract file for each payer with the contract, rate sheets, plan contacts and updates. Billing Staff update the file whenever the plan changes a rate or billing instruction.

If a patient asks about CDPAP, the supervising RN explains that PPL is the Statewide Fiscal Intermediary and that this agency does not serve as a CDPAP fiscal intermediary. The RN refers the patient to the plan or care manager, or to the local district, and documents the referral.

The agency follows the district's or plan's determination about whether CDPAP, a personal emergency response service, shared aide or other services are more appropriate than the agency's personal care (18 NYCRR 505.14(b)(2)(iii)). Where staff think another service may be better, the RN raises that with the plan or district in writing. The agency does not make that determination.
Billing Staff bill only for services that are authorized, delivered and documented, and follow the compliance requirements in GOV-05.

The RN Director of Patient Services reports to the QI Committee on any recurring problems with authorizations, delays by plans or districts, and gaps between authorized and delivered hours (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Negotiates and signs payer contracts, requests contract-limit exceptions where needed, maintains the contract file, and confirms that wage pass-through and wage parity terms are met.
Reviews authorizations against assessments, orders and plans of care, and sets the clinical process for communicating with plans and districts.
Reconciles the plan of care with authorizations, communicates changes in need to the plan or district, and refers patients who want CDPAP.
Collect payer information and authorizations at referral and keep care manager contact information current.
Reconcile authorized hours with delivered hours and bill only for authorized, delivered and documented services.

documentation: Copy of the authorization and plan of care showing level, amount, frequency and duration
Payer and care manager contact record
Written requests to the plan or district for changes in services
Notes of communication with plan care managers about changes, reductions and reassessments
Referral note for patients who ask about CDPAP
Signed MLTC contracts with rate, billing codes and units, authorization process and wage pass-through terms
Contract-limit exception correspondence, where applicable
Monthly authorized versus delivered hours reconciliation

policies.title: Introduction of New Services and Procedures (QI Committee Review)
policies.applies_to: The RN Director of Patient Services, supervising RNs, the QI Committee, the governing authority and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure that no new nursing or therapeutic service, procedure or treatment is introduced into patients' homes until the QI Committee has reviewed it, so that new care is safe, appropriate and delivered by trained staff.
policies.policy: Any nursing or therapeutic service, procedure or treatment that [AGENCY NAME] has not previously provided in patients' homes is first reviewed by the QI Committee (10 NYCRR §766.2(a)(7)). The agency does not begin the service until the Committee has completed its review and the governing authority has approved it, with one exception. If a patient needs the service urgently, it may be implemented before QI review, but only if medical consultation on the safety and appropriateness of the service was obtained and the staff who will provide it are trained for that specific service. The QI Committee is the committee described in 10 NYCRR §766.9(l), and it reviews the agency's policies as part of its function. Adding services or counties to the agency's license is a separate DOH amendment process, described in GOV-02, and is not replaced by this policy.

definitions.definition: A nursing or therapeutic service, procedure or treatment that the agency has not previously provided in homes.
The quality improvement committee, including a consumer and health professionals, that meets at least four times a year and reports in writing to the governing authority.
A situation in which waiting for the next scheduled QI Committee review would put the patient's health or safety at risk or would prevent the patient from receiving needed care.
A filing with the NYS Department of Health to add counties, services or sites to the agency's license; it is separate from QI review.

procedures: Any staff member who believes the agency should provide a new service, procedure or treatment sends a written proposal to the RN Director of Patient Services. The proposal describes the service, why it is needed and who would provide it.

The RN Director of Patient Services decides whether the proposal is a new nursing or therapeutic service, procedure or treatment for the agency. If there is any doubt, the RN Director treats it as new and sends it for QI review.

The RN Director of Patient Services prepares a review packet for the QI Committee. The packet describes the service and procedure, the patient population, the practitioner order requirements, the staff qualifications and training needed, the equipment and supplies, infection control requirements (see SAF-03), the clinical risks and the documentation needed in the patient care record.

The RN Director of Patient Services confirms that the service falls within the agency's licensed services. If the service would require a change to the agency's license, the Administrator starts the separate amendment process in GOV-02. The agency does not provide the service until DOH has approved the amendment.

The QI Committee reviews the packet at its next meeting, or at a special meeting called by the Chair if the matter cannot wait. The Committee records its recommendation to approve, approve with conditions, or decline.
The Committee sends its recommendation to the governing authority in writing. The governing authority decides whether to adopt the new service and any related policy (see GOV-01 and GOV-03).

If the service is approved, the RN Director of Patient Services writes or revises the policy and procedure for the service and has the Committee confirm it. The policy is added to the manual under GOV-03.

Before any staff member provides the service, the RN Director of Patient Services trains the staff for that specific service and documents a competency evaluation (see PER-03). Only staff who have completed the training and who are within their legal scope of practice may provide it.

Where a patient needs the new service urgently, the RN Director of Patient Services may authorize implementation before QI review only after confirming that medical consultation on the safety and appropriateness of the service has been obtained and documented, and that the staff who will provide it are trained for that specific service.

For any urgent implementation, the RN Director of Patient Services documents in the patient care record the urgent need, the medical consultation (who, when and what was advised), and the staff training, and keeps a record of the urgent implementation for the QI Committee.

The RN Director of Patient Services reports every urgent implementation to the QI Committee at its next meeting. The Committee then completes the review in this policy, and any conditions it sets apply from that date.
Supervising RNs monitor the first patients receiving the new service through in-home supervisory visits (see SVC-07), and report outcomes and problems to the RN Director of Patient Services.
The QI Committee reviews the first reports on outcomes for the new service at a following meeting and includes the service in its record sample (see GOV-04).
The Administrator keeps the proposal, review packet, Committee minutes, governing authority decision, training records and any urgent-use documentation in the QI file.

responsibilities.duty: Reviews each proposed new service, procedure or treatment before it is introduced, and reviews any urgent implementation afterwards.
Receives the Committee's written recommendation, decides whether to adopt the new service and approves the related policy.
Prepares review packets, confirms staff training and competency, authorizes urgent implementation only where the conditions are met, and monitors outcomes.
Confirms whether a license amendment is required, starts the amendment process, and maintains the QI file.
Monitors care for the first patients receiving a new service and reports problems to the RN Director of Patient Services.

documentation: Written proposal for the new service
QI review packet
QI Committee minutes and recommendation
Governing authority decision
New or revised policy and procedure
Staff training and competency records for the new service
For urgent implementation: documentation of the urgent need, the medical consultation and the staff training
Follow-up outcome reports to the QI Committee

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME], including personal care aides, supervising RNs, office staff, the RN Director of Patient Services and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To protect patients from abuse, neglect, mistreatment and financial exploitation by preventing harm through careful hiring, training and supervision, and by making sure that every concern is reported, investigated, documented and addressed.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect, mistreatment or exploitation of patients by anyone. The agency adopts this policy under the authority of its governing authority to set policies and to be responsible for the operation of the agency and compliance with the law (10 NYCRR §766.9(b), (d)). The agency's review of Part 766 did not locate a section that prescribes an abuse-reporting procedure or deadline for home care services agencies. The timelines in this policy are therefore set by the agency, and they are not state-prescribed deadlines. The agency screens prospective employees with a criminal history record check (10 NYCRR §402.6), a Home Care Registry check and employment and reference verification before patient contact. Patients may complain without reprisal and are told how to contact the Department of Health (10 NYCRR §766.1(a)(8)-(9)). All allegations and incidents are documented in the patient care record (10 NYCRR §766.6(a)(8)). The Administrator confirms with legal counsel the current New York mandated-reporter duties and the Adult Protective Services referral process that apply to the agency, and the agency updates this policy accordingly.

definitions.definition: Any willful act or omission that causes or is likely to cause physical, sexual, verbal or emotional harm to a patient, including hitting, restraining, threatening, humiliating, or sexual contact of any kind.

Failure to provide care, supervision or services that a patient needs to be safe and healthy, including leaving a patient who needs supervision, withholding food, medication assistance or help with hygiene, or failing to report a hazard.

Improper use of a patient's money, property, identity or resources for the benefit of someone else, including theft, forged checks, coercion to give gifts or loans, and misuse of a patient's cards or accounts.
Inappropriate treatment of a patient that does not meet the definition of abuse or neglect, including disrespectful treatment or ignoring the patient's rights.
The local social services district program that receives referrals about adults who may be at risk of harm and who cannot protect themselves.

procedures: Prevention at hire: Human Resources requests a criminal history record check for each prospective employee, submits the signed DOH form and two sets of fingerprints within 10 business days of taking the prints, resubmits within 14 days of notice that prints were rejected, and follows the supervision requirements for any temporary approval (10 NYCRR §402.6; see PER-02).

Prevention at hire: Human Resources checks the Home Care Registry, verifies identity, and verifies employment history and references before the aide has patient contact (see PER-02 and PER-09). Anyone with a disqualifying history or an unresolved question is not assigned to patients until the Administrator has reviewed it.

Prevention in training: the agency trains all staff at orientation and annually on recognizing and reporting abuse, neglect and exploitation, on professional boundaries and on the patient's right to complain without reprisal (see PER-03, PER-07 and CR-04).
Prevention in care: supervising RNs watch for warning signs during in-home supervisory visits and aide supervision, and ask patients privately about how they are treated (see SVC-07).

Informing patients: at the start of care, the agency gives each patient the written statement of patient rights, which includes the right to be treated with respect, to complain free of reprisal and to contact the DOH. The agency documents receipt in the patient care record (10 NYCRR §766.1(a); see CR-01).

Immediate safety: any staff member who sees or suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation, or who is told about it, first makes sure the patient is safe. If anyone is in immediate danger, the staff member calls 911.

Reporting inside the agency: the staff member reports every suspicion or allegation to the supervising RN, or the RN Director of Patient Services, immediately and in any case by the end of the shift, regardless of who is accused. If the report concerns the RN Director of Patient Services, the staff member reports to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME]. If it concerns the Administrator, the staff member reports to the governing authority at [PHONE].

No staff member may investigate alone, confront the accused, promise the patient to keep the matter secret, or delay reporting because they are unsure. Reports may be made orally or in writing, and may be made anonymously.

Supervisor action: the supervising RN or RN Director of Patient Services notifies [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] the same day. They arrange for any needed medical attention and, with the Administrator, take immediate steps to protect the patient. These steps include removing the accused from contact with the patient and from other patients pending review.

External reporting: the RN Director of Patient Services and the Administrator decide the same day whether the matter must be referred to Adult Protective Services, law enforcement, the Medicaid managed care plan, the Department of Health or another authority. They use the requirements confirmed with legal counsel, and they document the decision, who was contacted, when and by what method.
Notice to the plan: for MLTC members, the supervising RN notifies the plan care manager the same business day, unless the plan has set a different timeline in its contract (see SVC-13).

Investigation: the Administrator, or a person designated by the Administrator who is not involved in the allegation, starts an investigation promptly and in any case within one business day. The investigator interviews the patient, the staff involved and witnesses, reviews records and visit data (see SVC-10), and keeps notes.

Protection from retaliation: no one may retaliate against a patient or staff member for making a report in good faith. Any retaliation is itself a violation of this policy and is subject to discipline up to termination (see CR-01 and CR-02).

Outcome: the Administrator completes a written investigation report within 14 calendar days when practicable, stating the findings, the actions taken and any report to outside authorities. Staff found to have committed abuse, neglect or exploitation are terminated. The agency makes any further reports required by law, which may include reports relating to the aide's registry entry (see PER-09).
Patient notification: the supervising RN informs the patient, or the patient's authorized representative, of the outcome as appropriate, and revises the plan of care if needed (see SVC-06).

Privacy: staff share information about an allegation only with those who need it to protect the patient, to investigate, or to make a report that is permitted or required by law (see CR-03; 45 CFR 164.512(c)). Staff do not discuss allegations with other patients, other staff or the public.

Billing integrity: if the investigation shows that a patient was billed for services not delivered because of abuse, neglect or exploitation, the Administrator refers the matter under the corporate compliance program (see GOV-05; 42 CFR 455.12-455.23).

QI review: the RN Director of Patient Services reports all substantiated and unsubstantiated allegations, with outcomes, to the QI Committee at least quarterly without patient names where practicable, and the Committee reviews patterns (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Owns this policy, confirms the mandated-reporter and APS requirements with legal counsel, ensures investigations are completed and decides on external reports with the RN Director of Patient Services.
Receives reports, protects the patient, coordinates medical attention, notifies the plan and APS as required, and reports patterns to the QI Committee.
Watches for signs of abuse or neglect during supervisory visits, receives staff reports and notifies the RN Director of Patient Services immediately.
Completes criminal history record checks, Registry checks, identity and reference verification before patient contact, and keeps the records.
Treat patients with respect, report any suspicion or allegation by the end of the shift, call 911 in an emergency and cooperate with investigations.
Receives reports about allegations against the Administrator and oversees the agency's response.

documentation: Criminal history record check requests, submission dates and results
Home Care Registry check, identity verification and reference verification records
Signed receipt of patient rights in the patient care record
Staff training records on abuse, neglect and exploitation
Incident or allegation report completed by the same business day
Entry in the patient care record documenting the allegation or incident (10 NYCRR §766.6(a)(8))
Record of external reports, including who was contacted, when and the method
Investigation notes and written investigation report
Record of disciplinary action and patient notification
Written confirmation from legal counsel of current mandated-reporter and APS requirements, with date

policies.title: Incident and Accident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All patient care staff, supervising RNs, the RN Director of Patient Services, the Administrator and the QI Committee
policies.purpose: To make sure that every incident or accident involving a patient or occurring in the course of care is reported promptly, documented, reviewed and used to improve patient safety.
policies.policy: Staff report every incident and accident to their supervisor, and the agency documents accidents and incidents in the patient care record (10 NYCRR §766.6(a)(8)). Changes in a patient's condition and problems with the patient's informal supports or home are reported to supervisory staff promptly, as part of the supervision the governing authority must ensure (10 NYCRR §766.5(b)). The QI Committee reviews incident patterns (10 NYCRR §766.9(l)). The agency's 24/7 Health Provider Network (HPN) contacts are used to receive DOH alerts (10 NYCRR §766.9(o)). The agency's review of Part 766 did not locate a deadline for reporting incidents to the Department of Health. The agency has therefore set its own internal timelines, below. The agency also confirms any additional reporting rules in each MLTC contract.

definitions.definition: Any unusual event involving a patient or staff member in the course of care that affects, or could affect, health or safety, including falls, injuries, medication errors or refusals, missing patients, property damage, threats, abuse allegations, patient deaths, aggressive behavior and exposures to blood or body fluids.
An unplanned event that results in injury or potential injury to a patient or staff member, such as a fall, burn, choking or equipment injury.
An event that could have caused harm but did not, which is reported so that the agency can prevent a recurrence.
An incident involving death, a injury needing emergency treatment or hospital admission, suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, a missing patient, or a threat of violence.
The Health Provider Network, the DOH electronic communication system used to receive alerts and to maintain 24/7 emergency contacts.

procedures: Immediate response: the staff member present attends to the safety of the patient. If there is a medical emergency or immediate danger, the staff member calls 911 and then follows SVC-11. The staff member does not move an injured patient except to prevent further harm.

Notice to the supervisor: the staff member telephones the supervising RN, or the on-call RN after hours, as soon as the patient is safe and in any case within one hour of a serious incident, and by the end of the shift for any other incident.

Notice to the RN Director of Patient Services: the supervising RN informs the RN Director of Patient Services the same day about any serious incident, and within one business day about all other incidents.
Notice to the Administrator: the RN Director of Patient Services informs [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] of every serious incident the same day.

Notice to the practitioner, family and plan: the supervising RN notifies the authorized practitioner as needed for the patient's condition. The RN also notifies the patient's representative or emergency contact, and for MLTC members the plan care manager, the same business day for any serious incident, unless the plan's contract sets a different time. The RN documents each notification.

Incident report: the staff member who witnessed or discovered the event completes the agency incident report by the end of the shift. The report states factual observations only: date, time, place, persons involved, what happened, injuries, actions taken, who was notified and names of witnesses.

Patient care record: the staff member and the supervising RN record the incident or accident in the patient care record, with date and signature, and note any change in the patient's condition (10 NYCRR §766.6(a)(8)). The incident report itself is kept in the agency's incident file, and is cross-referenced in the record.

Supervisory follow-up: the supervising RN evaluates the patient, in person where the incident involved injury or a change in condition, within 24 hours or at the next available time. The RN reviews the plan of care, revises it if needed and instructs the aide (see SVC-06 and SVC-07).

Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation: any incident that raises such a suspicion is also handled under SAF-01. Incidents involving exposure to blood or body fluids are handled under SAF-07. Incidents of violence against staff are handled under SAF-06.

Staff injuries: a staff member who is injured reports to the supervisor immediately. The agency arranges care, completes any required workers' compensation forms, and documents in the personnel file, kept separate from the patient record.

Evaluation: within five business days of a serious incident, and within 14 days of any other incident, the RN Director of Patient Services reviews the report, determines the cause and contributing factors, and decides on corrective action, such as retraining, equipment changes or a plan of care revision.

External reports: the RN Director of Patient Services and the Administrator decide whether the incident must be reported to the Department of Health, APS, law enforcement, the plan or another body. They check the applicable MLTC contract and legal requirements, and document the decision and the report (see REC-02). If a DOH alert is received through HPN, the 24/7 emergency contact responds under GOV-07.
Incident log: the RN Director of Patient Services keeps an incident log that records, for each incident, the date, the type, the patient and staff involved, the actions taken and the closure date.

QI review: at each meeting, which occurs at least four times a year, the QI Committee reviews the incident log for patterns by type, location, time, staff and patient, and recommends system changes (10 NYCRR §766.9(l); see GOV-04).
Follow-up on corrective actions: the RN Director of Patient Services tracks each corrective action to completion and reports overdue actions to the Administrator.
Retention: incident reports and the log are kept under the schedule in REC-03, and patient care record entries are kept under REC-01.

responsibilities.role: Personal Care Aide and other care staff
responsibilities.duty: Make the patient safe, call 911 when needed, report the incident to the supervisor within the stated times and complete an incident report factually.
Evaluates the patient, notifies the practitioner, the family and the plan, records the incident in the patient care record, and updates the plan of care.
Reviews and classifies every incident, determines corrective action, decides on external reports with the Administrator and keeps the incident log.
Receives serious incident reports the same day, makes external reporting decisions and makes sure that corrective actions are completed.
Reviews incident patterns at least quarterly and recommends system improvements.

documentation: Agency incident report completed by the end of the shift
Dated and signed patient care record entry documenting the accident or incident (10 NYCRR §766.6(a)(8))
Notification record for the practitioner, family or representative and the plan
Supervisory visit note and plan of care revision where needed
Incident log
Record of external reports and the decision about whether to report
Corrective action tracking record
QI Committee minutes showing incident review

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All personnel with direct patient contact, supervising RNs, the RN Director of Patient Services, Human Resources and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of infection among patients and staff through written procedures for cleaning and disinfection, employee immunization and tuberculosis screening, standard precautions and exposure management.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains written procedures for the storage, cleaning and disinfection of supplies, equipment and appliances used in patient care (10 NYCRR §766.2(a)(5)). All personnel with direct patient contact must meet the health requirements of 10 NYCRR §766.11(d): a tuberculosis (TB) risk assessment, symptom evaluation and TB test before employment and annually, with a written policy on follow-up of positive results; documented measles and rubella immunity; and annual influenza vaccination documentation, or a surgical or procedure mask during the influenza season for those who are not vaccinated. Medical exemption statements are kept in the personnel health record. The agency's bloodborne pathogen program meets 10 NYCRR §766.11(l) and 29 CFR 1910.1030 and is set out in SAF-07.

definitions.definition: Infection prevention practices applied to all patients, including hand hygiene, use of gloves and other personal protective equipment, safe handling of sharps, and cleaning and disinfection of surfaces and equipment.
Gloves, masks, gowns, eye protection and other barriers that protect staff and patients from infectious materials.
Use of a suitable product to kill most disease-causing organisms on surfaces and equipment, following the product's label for contact time and use.
Work that involves being in the patient's presence, or handling items or surfaces that the patient uses, in the course of providing care.
A written statement from a licensed practitioner that an immunization is medically contraindicated, kept in the employee's health record.

procedures: Before an employee has patient contact, Human Resources collects documentation of rubella immunity and of measles immunity (for staff born on or after 1/1/1957), as required by 10 NYCRR §766.11(d). Where the employee has no documentation, the agency arranges testing or vaccination before patient contact.

Before the employee has patient contact, the employee completes a TB risk assessment, symptom evaluation and TB test. The employee repeats the assessment and TB test annually. Results are placed in the confidential employee health record, kept separate from the personnel file (see PER-04 and PER-05).

The agency maintains a written follow-up procedure for a positive TB test or symptoms. The employee is referred immediately to a licensed practitioner, is removed from patient contact until cleared in writing, and returns only with the practitioner's written clearance, which is filed in the health record.

Each year before the influenza season, Human Resources collects documentation of influenza vaccination from each employee with direct patient contact. An employee who is not vaccinated must wear a surgical or procedure mask when in patient contact during the influenza season, and the agency notifies staff when the season begins and ends.

Employees with a medical exemption provide a written statement from a licensed practitioner. Human Resources files the statement in the health record and applies the mask requirement where the exemption relates to influenza vaccination.

Orientation and annual training: the agency trains each aide on standard precautions, hand hygiene, PPE use, cleaning and disinfection, safe handling of soiled linen and waste, and when to report possible infection (see PER-03).

Hand hygiene: staff wash hands with soap and water, or use an alcohol-based hand rub where hands are not visibly soiled, before and after each patient contact, before and after glove use, after toileting or incontinence care, after contact with body fluids, and before preparing food.

PPE: staff wear gloves when contact with blood, body fluids, nonintact skin or contaminated surfaces is likely, and use gowns, masks or eye protection when splashes are likely. The agency makes PPE available to staff at no cost, and staff dispose of PPE after use and do not reuse single-use items.

Cleaning and disinfection: staff clean and disinfect shared equipment and appliances, such as commodes, bathing aids and thermometers, between uses, and follow the written procedure approved by the RN Director of Patient Services, using products as labeled. Supplies are stored clean and dry, separate from soiled items, and are checked for damage and expiry.

Soiled linen and waste: staff handle soiled linen and waste with gloves, bag them securely and keep them separate from clean items. Sharps are not part of an aide's duties (see SVC-01) but, if encountered, are never handled by the aide and are reported to the supervising RN.

Staff illness: staff with fever, vomiting, diarrhea, rash or other signs of a contagious illness, or with a known exposure, notify the supervisor before the shift. The supervisor decides on work restrictions with the RN Director of Patient Services, and the scheduler arranges coverage while preserving continuity as far as possible (see SVC-09).

Patient illness: if a patient has signs of infection, the aide reports to the supervising RN the same day, and the RN evaluates the patient and notifies the practitioner as needed (see SVC-11). Where a patient has a known communicable condition, the RN gives the aide specific precautions, documents them in the plan of care and confirms the aide's understanding.
Exposures: an exposure to blood or body fluids is handled under SAF-07, which sets out the exposure-management procedure and medical follow-up.
Monitoring: the supervising RN observes hand hygiene, PPE use and cleaning technique during supervisory visits, and records observations (see SVC-07).

Tracking: Human Resources keeps a compliance tracker of each employee's TB test, immunity documentation and influenza status, and reviews it monthly. Employees who are overdue are not scheduled for patient contact until compliant.
QI review: the RN Director of Patient Services reports infection-related incidents, staff illness and compliance rates to the QI Committee at least quarterly (see GOV-04).
Review: the RN Director of Patient Services reviews this policy and the cleaning and disinfection procedures at least annually (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Approves infection control procedures, directs staff training, decides on work restrictions with Human Resources and reports infection data to the QI Committee.
Collects and tracks TB, immunity and influenza documentation, keeps health records separate and confidential and keeps non-compliant staff off patient contact.
Observes infection control practice, instructs aides on patient-specific precautions and evaluates patients with signs of infection.
Follows standard precautions, uses PPE, cleans and disinfects equipment, and reports illness and exposures promptly.
Provides PPE and cleaning supplies at no cost to staff and makes sure the program is implemented and reviewed.

documentation: Rubella and measles immunity documentation in the employee health record
TB risk assessment, symptom evaluation and TB test results, before employment and annually
Written TB follow-up procedure and practitioner clearances
Annual influenza vaccination documentation or mask-wearing record
Medical exemption statements
Infection control training and competency records
Written procedures for storage, cleaning and disinfection of supplies, equipment and appliances
Supervisory visit observations of infection control practice
Compliance tracker and QI Committee reports

policies.title: Client Emergency and Disaster Plans
policies.applies_to: All patients, the RN Director of Patient Services, supervising RNs, scheduling staff and aides
policies.purpose: To make sure each patient's care continues, or a safe alternative is arranged, when an emergency interferes with service delivery. This includes severe weather, power loss, public health events, transportation shutdowns and building emergencies.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] plans for each patient's continued care during emergencies that interfere with service delivery (10 NYCRR §766.9(c)). The RN identifies patients with a high need for uninterrupted care, records an emergency contact and an individual emergency plan in each patient's record, and reviews both when the patient's condition or situation changes. All staff are oriented to their responsibilities in the emergency plan. The agency uses its Health Provider Network (HPN) account and its 24/7 emergency contacts to receive Department of Health emergency communications (§766.9(o)). No patient is left without a plan, and an aide never leaves a patient who is unsafe alone.

definitions.definition: A patient whose health or safety would be put at risk by a missed or delayed visit, as determined by the RN. Examples are patients who cannot get out of bed or a chair without help, who cannot summon help, who have dementia or cognitive impairment, who depend on electricity-powered equipment, or who live alone with no informal supports.
A person the patient names, other than the agency, who can be called in an emergency and who can help the patient evacuate or shelter.
The Department of Health's Health Provider Network, used for emergency alerts and for agency contact information (§766.9(o)).

procedures: At intake, the admitting RN asks each patient or representative for at least one emergency contact with a working phone number and records it in the patient record (see SVC-02).

During the RN's initial assessment, the RN evaluates the patient's dependence on caregivers, mobility, cognition, ability to call for help, medical equipment and living arrangements. The RN designates the patient as high-need, standard-need or lower-need and records the rating and reason.

The RN writes an individual emergency plan for each patient. It states who the patient would call, where the patient would shelter or evacuate, what equipment or medication the patient needs, how the patient would get transportation, and whether the patient has a pet or service animal.

For high-need patients, the plan also states the order in which the patient is called or visited when service is disrupted, and whether the patient should be referred to the MLTC plan care manager or local emergency management for special-needs registration. The RN offers to help the patient register where such registries exist.
The RN reviews the plan with the patient or representative and gives them the agency's 24/7 phone number, [PHONE]. The patient's acknowledgment is documented.

The RN reviews the emergency contact and plan at each supervisory visit, at reassessment, and when a change in condition, address or living situation occurs (see SVC-07 and SVC-11). Updates are dated and signed.
The scheduling supervisor keeps a current list of high-need patients, their aides, their emergency contacts and their addresses. The list is accessible after hours to the on-call RN.

When a weather or other emergency is forecast or begins, the RN Director of Patient Services or designee activates the agency emergency plan (SAF-05) and notifies on-call staff. The designee also checks HPN and Department of Health communications for alerts and directions.

Before the event, if time allows, the RN or scheduler calls all high-need patients to confirm that they are safe, that their plan is still workable and that their aide's schedule is known. Calls and outcomes are logged.

During the event, staff call patients in priority order, high-need first. If an aide cannot reach a patient, the aide calls the scheduler. The scheduler arranges a replacement aide, a different visit time, a welfare check through the emergency contact, or a call to 911 or local authorities if the patient may be in danger.

The agency never discontinues service to a high-need patient without confirming that someone else is present or that the patient has been safely transferred. Any gap in care is reported to the supervising RN immediately.

Aides who are with a patient when an emergency begins stay with the patient until relieved or until the patient is safely placed, unless their own safety is at risk. They follow the patient's plan and call the on-call RN at [PHONE].

The on-call RN logs every emergency-related missed or altered visit and notifies the MLTC plan or the local district when required (see SVC-13). The RN reports any patient injury or harm as an incident (SAF-02).

Within 7 days after the emergency ends, the RN Director of Patient Services reviews how patient plans worked, lists problems and corrective actions, and takes the review to the next QI Committee meeting (GOV-04).

Orientation for every new employee includes the patient emergency procedures in this policy. Staff sign that they have been oriented, and the orientation is repeated whenever the plan changes (see PER-03).

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure each patient has a documented emergency contact and plan, keeps the high-need list current, activates patient emergency procedures and reviews results after each event.
Assesses need for uninterrupted care, writes and updates the individual emergency plan, and makes priority calls during an event.
Keeps the contact and high-need lists, reassigns visits during disruptions and logs all outreach.
Knows the patient's plan, stays with the patient when appropriate, and calls the agency promptly if a visit cannot be made or the patient is in danger.
Makes sure HPN contacts are current and that the agency has the resources to carry out the plan.

documentation: Emergency contact and individual emergency plan in the patient record
High-need patient list with dates of review
Emergency call logs and missed or altered visit documentation
Orientation sign-in sheets for emergency procedures
Post-event review and QI Committee minutes

policies.title: Agency Emergency Plan and Continuity of Operations
policies.applies_to: Governing authority, Administrator, RN Director of Patient Services, office staff and all employees
policies.purpose: To keep the agency operating, and its patients' health care needs met, during an emergency that interferes with service delivery. It also protects patient and personnel records and provides for orderly closure.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a current written emergency plan with procedures to ensure that patients' health care needs continue to be met in emergencies that interfere with service delivery. The plan is reviewed at least annually. All employees are oriented to the plan (10 NYCRR §766.9(c)). The agency keeps an adequate office with prompt phone contact and arranges so that professional staff can reach patient records (§766.9(f)). Electronic records are backed up in a secure and confidential manner and can be printed on request (§766.12(b)). If the agency closes, it arranges for the safe storage of its records and notifies the Department of Health in writing where they are kept.

definitions.definition: The agency's written procedures for keeping care going when an emergency interferes with service delivery. It covers staffing, communication, records, supplies and alternate work locations.
The ability of the agency to schedule, supervise, document and bill for services during and after a disruption.

procedures: The Administrator and RN Director of Patient Services write and maintain the agency emergency plan. It covers the hazards most likely to affect [AGENCY NAME] and its counties served, including severe weather, power or internet outage, pandemic or infectious disease outbreak, fire, loss of the office, and cyber events.

The plan names an incident commander and a back-up for each shift. It lists the 24/7 emergency contacts, key staff phone numbers, the Department of Health and local emergency management contacts, and the MLTC plans and payers to be notified.

The plan sets out how the agency communicates with staff and patients: phone tree, text or app alerts, and a recorded message at [PHONE] if the office is unavailable. It also includes a back-up method if phones or internet fail.

The plan provides for staffing during an emergency. It covers on-call RN coverage, cross-trained schedulers, an aide availability list, and rules for reassigning aides to high-need patients first (see SAF-04).

The plan identifies an alternate work location, which may be remote work for office staff, and the equipment and access needed to run it. [ADDRESS] is the primary office; the alternate location is recorded in the plan.

Professional staff keep access to patient records at all times. Paper records are stored in locked cabinets away from flood or fire risk. Electronic records are stored on a secure system with access limits, and are backed up on a regular schedule at a secure off-site or cloud location. Back-up restoration is tested at least annually.
The Administrator confirms that records can be printed or exported on request and that the on-call RN can see each high-need patient's plan and contacts after hours.
Every new employee is oriented to the emergency plan during orientation, and existing employees are re-oriented when the plan changes and at least annually. Sign-in sheets are kept (see PER-03).
The agency tests the plan at least once a year with a drill or tabletop exercise. The results and corrective actions are documented and presented to the QI Committee.
The Administrator reviews the plan at least annually and after any actual emergency. Changes are approved under GOV-03 and the dated revision is placed in the policy manual.

When an emergency occurs, the incident commander activates the plan, notifies the RN Director of Patient Services, begins patient outreach under SAF-04 and checks HPN and Department of Health communications for instructions. Actions are time-stamped in an event log.
If the office is unusable, the Administrator moves operations to the alternate location, forwards the main phone line, and notifies staff and payers within the time frame set in the plan.

After the emergency, the Administrator completes an after-action report listing what happened, patient impact, gaps in care, and corrections. The report is shared with the governing authority and the QI Committee (GOV-04).

If the agency decides to close or cannot continue operating, the governing authority first arranges the safe transfer of patients to other providers (SVC-12). It then arranges for the retention and secure storage of patient and personnel records for the required periods (REC-01 and REC-03) and notifies the Department of Health in writing of the location of the stored records and the person who can provide access.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts the emergency plan, reviews it annually and decides on closure and record storage.
Maintains the plan, tests it annually, protects the office and records, and notifies the Department of Health and payers.
Directs patient care continuity, on-call RN coverage and patient outreach during an emergency.
Follow the plan, keep communication lists current and log actions.
Complete orientation to the plan and follow instructions during an emergency.

documentation: Written emergency plan with review and revision dates
Orientation records for all employees
Annual drill or tabletop exercise report
Records back-up and restoration test logs
After-action reports and QI Committee minutes
Written notice to DOH of records location, if the agency closes

policies.title: Caregiver Safety in the Home and Workplace Violence
policies.applies_to: All aides, supervising RNs, office staff and any employee who visits a patient's home
policies.purpose: To protect employees from hazards in patients' homes and the workplace, including unsafe conditions, aggression and violence. It also makes sure that problems with the home environment are found, reported and addressed.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] works to provide a workplace free from recognized hazards likely to cause death or serious harm, consistent with the OSHA General Duty Clause (29 USC 654). Supervisory staff review problems with the patient's home environment and informal supports as part of supervision (10 NYCRR §766.5(b)(3)), and personal protective equipment appropriate to the tasks is provided to employees (§766.11(l)(1)(iv)). Employees may leave an unsafe situation and report it without penalty. The agency does not tolerate violence, threats or harassment against employees by anyone, including patients, family members and co-workers. No New York Part 766 section on workplace violence was located; this policy is an agency standard.

definitions.definition: Any physical assault, threatening behavior or verbal abuse directed at an employee while working, in the patient's home, in the community or at the agency office.

A hazard in the home that threatens the aide's health or safety. Examples are infestation, lack of heat, unsafe wiring, unsecured weapons, aggressive animals, active drug use, smoking near oxygen, or a person who is threatening.

procedures: At intake, the RN completes a home safety assessment, including the physical environment, pets, smoking, firearms or weapons, other household members, neighborhood, access, and known behavioral risks. The RN documents findings in the patient record (SVC-02).

The RN gives the aide a safety briefing before the first visit. It covers hazards identified, behavioral concerns, directions to the home, and the contact numbers to call, including the on-call RN at [PHONE]. Details are on the aide's assignment sheet and plan of care.

The RN reviews the home environment and informal supports at every supervisory visit and when the aide reports a problem. Problems are recorded and the plan of care or service is revised as needed (SVC-06 and SVC-07).

The agency provides PPE suited to the tasks, such as gloves, masks, gowns and eye protection, at no cost to the employee. Employees are trained in its use and replace used items as needed (SAF-03 and SAF-07).

Aides are told at orientation that they have the right to leave a home immediately if they feel in danger. They must go to a safe place and call 911 if there is imminent danger, then call the agency as soon as it is safe.

An aide who is threatened, assaulted or harassed must report it to the supervising RN or on-call RN by phone as soon as safe, and no later than the end of the shift. The employee completes an incident report within 24 hours (SAF-02).

The RN or Administrator contacts the aide promptly, checks on the aide's well-being, arranges medical care if needed, and arranges a replacement aide or modified schedule so the patient's care is not interrupted.

The RN assesses the cause of the incident. If it relates to the patient's condition (for example dementia), the RN reviews the plan of care, refers the patient to the practitioner or MLTC plan, and gives the aide strategies. If it is caused by a household member or visitor, the Administrator decides what protections are needed.

If the risk cannot be controlled, the RN Director of Patient Services and the Administrator may suspend service, assign two staff, or begin discharge or transfer under SVC-12. The patient and payer are notified as required, and the patient is not abandoned.
The agency reports crimes to law enforcement and, where abuse or neglect of the patient is suspected, follows SAF-01. Reports to the MLTC plan or the local district are made under SVC-13.
The agency does not retaliate against any employee who reports a hazard, leaves an unsafe home or reports violence. Retaliation is grounds for discipline.
Employees are trained at orientation and annually on home safety, de-escalation, recognizing warning signs, personal safety when traveling to and from visits, and how to report (PER-03).

The Administrator reviews all workplace violence and unsafe-home reports at least quarterly, looks for trends, and presents a summary to the QI Committee (GOV-04). Corrective actions are recorded and followed up.
Employees injured at work are directed to report the injury immediately so that workers' compensation and any OSHA recordkeeping required for the employer can be handled.

responsibilities.duty: Provides PPE and training, enforces non-retaliation, decides on service suspension and reviews incident trends.

responsibilities.role: RN Director of Patient Services / supervising RN
responsibilities.duty: Assesses the home, briefs aides, responds to reports, revises plans and supports employees after an incident.
Follows safety instructions, uses PPE, leaves unsafe situations and reports hazards and incidents promptly.
Answers safety calls 24/7 and directs the response.

documentation: Home safety assessment in the patient record
Aide safety briefing acknowledgment
Incident reports and follow-up notes
PPE issue and training records
Quarterly trend review and QI Committee minutes

policies.title: Bloodborne Pathogen and Significant-Risk Body Substance Exposure Program
policies.applies_to: All employees with potential contact with blood or body substances, the RN Director of Patient Services and the designated exposure contact
policies.purpose: To reduce the risk of exposure to bloodborne pathogens and other significant-risk body substances, and to make sure any exposure is promptly reported, evaluated and followed up.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a bloodborne pathogen program as required by 10 NYCRR §766.11(l). It covers protective barriers, safe practices for handling contaminated equipment, training at hire and yearly, personal protective equipment, and monitoring. It also includes a procedure for managing exposures. The program is also designed to meet the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030. Exposure reports are kept confidential.

definitions.definition: Contact of an employee's broken skin, mucous membrane, or a needlestick or other sharps injury with blood or other body substances capable of transmitting infection, as identified in the agency's exposure control plan.
The person whose blood or body substance was the source of the exposure.
The agency staff member to whom exposures are reported: the RN Director of Patient Services or a designee named in the exposure control plan.

procedures: The RN Director of Patient Services writes and maintains an exposure control plan that identifies job roles with potential exposure, the tasks involved, and the protective measures for each. The plan is reviewed at least annually.

The agency provides protective barriers and PPE at no cost to employees. These include gloves, gowns, masks, eye protection, puncture-resistant sharps containers and cleaning supplies. Supplies are replaced on request.

Employees are trained at hire, before any contact with patients, and at least yearly. Training covers modes of transmission, standard precautions, safe handling of contaminated linens, equipment and waste, correct use of PPE, and what to do after an exposure. Training records are kept (PER-03).

Employees use standard precautions with all patients. They wear gloves for contact with blood or body fluids, wash hands as directed in SAF-03, and place any sharps, if the patient has them, only in approved containers without recapping or bending needles.
Contaminated equipment and surfaces are cleaned and disinfected using the agency's approved procedure. Contaminated waste is bagged and disposed of as the plan directs.
The agency offers hepatitis B vaccination to employees at risk, as required by the federal standard. Employees who decline sign a declination, which they may reverse at any time.

An employee who has an exposure immediately washes the area with soap and water or flushes mucous membranes with water. The employee then reports the exposure to the designated person right away, and no later than the end of the shift.

The designated person evaluates the exposure at once. The evaluation covers the circumstances, the type of body substance, the route of contact and the PPE used, and is documented on an exposure report.

The designated person arranges prompt medical evaluation and follow-up for the exposed employee, including counseling, testing as appropriate, and preventive treatment, with the employee's consent. Because some treatments work best when started quickly, the agency does not wait for the source individual's test results.

The designated person assesses the source individual's status where it is known or can be obtained lawfully. The source individual is offered counseling and voluntary testing. The agency does not require a patient to be tested.

The source individual's HIV-related information is disclosed to the exposed employee or their health care provider only with the source's express written consent or by court order. Staff do not discuss the source with anyone else.

Exposure reports and the exposed employee's medical records are kept confidential, are stored separately from the personnel file (PER-05), and are shared only with those who need them for follow-up or as the law requires.

The designated person records the exposure on the sharps injury or exposure log as the federal standard requires, and completes an incident report under SAF-02. The employee's follow-up is tracked until complete.

The RN Director of Patient Services reviews all exposures at least quarterly to find causes and prevent recurrence. A summary without identifying details goes to the QI Committee (GOV-04), and the exposure control plan is revised as needed.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the exposure control plan, serves as or names the designated person, and monitors the program.
Provides PPE and funding for training, vaccination and post-exposure follow-up.
Use standard precautions and PPE, complete training and report exposures immediately.
Receives reports, arranges evaluation and follow-up, and protects confidentiality.

documentation: Written exposure control plan with annual review
Training records at hire and yearly
Hepatitis B vaccine offers, acceptances and declinations
Exposure reports, sharps injury or exposure log, and follow-up records
Confidential medical records kept separate from personnel files
Quarterly exposure review

policies.title: Errands, Escort and Client Transportation
policies.applies_to: Personal care aides, schedulers, supervising RNs and the RN Director of Patient Services
policies.purpose: To make sure errands and escort are performed only when authorized, within the aide's permitted tasks, and with safe handling of the patient's money and transportation.
policies.policy: Aides at [AGENCY NAME] perform errands and escort only as listed in the authorized plan of care. Under 18 NYCRR §505.14(a)(5)(i)(a)(6) and (8), Level I services include shopping if no other arrangements are possible and essential errands. Level II services include walking within and outside the home (§505.14(a)(5)(ii)(a)(5)). The agency has no state rule on driving patients; this policy sets the agency's own standards. Aides do not drive patients in their own or the patient's vehicle unless the Administrator has approved it in writing and the conditions below are met.

definitions.definition: A task done outside the home on the patient's behalf, such as shopping for food or essential items, that is included in the authorized plan of care.
Accompanying the patient outside the home, for example walking with the patient, as authorized in the plan of care.
Driving the patient in a motor vehicle. This is outside the agency's standard scope unless approved under this policy.

procedures: At intake and at each plan update, the RN reviews the tasks authorized and ordered, and lists any shopping, errands or escort in the plan of care only if they fall within the authorized Level I or Level II tasks (SVC-01 and SVC-06).

The RN records the purpose, frequency and destination for each errand or escort, and checks that other arrangements (family, friends, delivery service) are not already available for shopping before the aide is assigned to it.

The aide receives the plan of care before the first visit and performs errands and escort only as written. If a patient asks for a task that is not in the plan, the aide declines politely and tells the supervising RN.

The aide uses the agency's money-handling procedure for any purchase (CR-04). The aide gets a receipt, records the amount given and the change returned, and has the patient or representative sign or initial the record. The aide does not use the patient's credit or debit cards, PINs or checks.

For walking and escort outside the home, the aide assesses the patient's safety before leaving, including weather, mobility needs and the use of walking aids. The aide stays with the patient and uses safe transfer and walking techniques taught in training.

Aides do not use a wheelchair van or other special equipment unless trained, and do not transport patients in any vehicle as part of routine services. If a patient needs a ride, the aide asks the RN or care manager to help arrange transportation through the patient's family, the MLTC plan or another community resource.

The Administrator may approve aide driving of a patient only in unusual circumstances.
