Competency checklists and return-demonstration records
Individual training record for each employee
Annual in-service calendar and attendance sheets
Bloodborne pathogen training record
Copies of aide qualifying training certificates
Training tracking report

policies.title: Employee Health, Immunization and TB Screening
policies.applies_to: All personnel with direct patient contact, and all new hires before they assume duties
policies.purpose: To protect patients and staff from preventable communicable disease and to make sure no one provides care while under a health impairment that endangers patients or interferes with duties.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] assesses and documents each employee's health status before the employee assumes patient care duties. No one assumes duties with a health impairment that poses a risk to patients or interferes with the performance of duties, including habituation or addiction to drugs or alcohol that may alter behavior (10 NYCRR §766.11(c)). For personnel with direct patient contact, the agency documents rubella immunity, measles immunity (for those born on or after 1/1/1957), TB screening before employment and annually, an annual health status assessment, and influenza vaccination or the wearing of a mask during influenza season (§766.11(d)). Health records are kept separate from the personnel file and are confidential (§766.11(g)).

definitions.definition: Any work that places the employee in the patient's home or in physical or close contact with patients.
A tuberculin skin test or an FDA-approved blood assay.
A written statement from a licensed practitioner that an immunization is medically contraindicated.
The period during which DOH requires unvaccinated direct-care personnel to wear masks.

procedures: As a condition of hire, each new employee with direct patient contact completes a health status assessment before the first patient assignment. The assessment is done by a licensed practitioner, or by the agency's designated RN reviewing the employee's practitioner-signed documentation. It is dated and kept in the confidential health file.

The assessment is limited to the employee's ability to perform the essential functions of the job, consistent with the ADA (42 USC 12112(d)). Medical information is gathered only after a conditional offer and is kept confidential.

The reviewing RN confirms the employee has no health impairment that is a risk to patients or interferes with duties, including drug or alcohol habituation or addiction that may alter behavior. If a concern exists, the RN Director of Patient Services and the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] consider reasonable accommodation and decide whether the employee may assume duties. The decision is recorded in the health file.
HR collects proof of rubella immunity (a certificate or laboratory evidence) for every employee with direct patient contact.
HR collects proof of measles immunity for every employee born on or after 1/1/1957. An employee with a medical contraindication provides a medical exemption statement from a licensed practitioner.

Before employment, each employee has an individual TB risk assessment, a symptom evaluation, and a TB test (skin test or FDA-approved blood assay). Results are documented before the first patient assignment.
Each year the employee has a TB risk assessment and education, and any additional testing the assessment calls for. The RN Director of Patient Services tracks due dates monthly.

The RN Director of Patient Services maintains a written follow-up protocol for positive TB results. It requires prompt referral for medical evaluation and removal from patient contact until a licensed practitioner documents that the employee is not infectious. Employees must report TB symptoms immediately.
Each year, every employee with direct patient contact has an annual health status assessment, documented in the health file.

Each year the employee provides documentation of influenza vaccination. An employee who is not vaccinated wears a mask during patient contact throughout the influenza season, as DOH requires. The RN Director of Patient Services announces the start and end of the season to staff in writing.
In keeping with 29 CFR 1910.1030(f), the agency offers hepatitis B vaccination at no cost to employees with occupational exposure. Declinations are signed and kept in the health file. See SAF-07.

HR keeps health records in a locked file or restricted electronic folder separate from the personnel file. Only the RN Director of Patient Services, the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], and HR staff designated in writing may see them. Information is shared with supervisors only as needed for work restrictions or accommodation.

Employees must report to the RN Director of Patient Services any illness or condition that may be communicable to patients. The RN Director decides on work restrictions and return to duty in consultation with the employee's practitioner.

HR runs a monthly report on upcoming and overdue health requirements. An employee whose required documentation is overdue past a written grace date set by the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] is taken off patient assignments until it is on file.

responsibilities.duty: Reviews health assessments, maintains the TB follow-up protocol, decides work restrictions, and announces influenza season masking.
Collects and files health documentation separately, and runs the monthly due-date report.
Approves accommodation and exclusion decisions and enforces the removal of employees with overdue requirements.
Complete health requirements on time and report symptoms and conditions that may be communicable.

documentation: Pre-employment health status assessment
Annual health status assessment
Rubella and measles immunity records or medical exemption statements
TB risk assessment, symptom evaluation, and test results (initial and annual)
TB follow-up written protocol and any case follow-up
Influenza vaccination record or masking acknowledgement
Hepatitis B vaccination or signed declination
Monthly health compliance report

policies.title: Personnel Records
policies.applies_to: HR/Personnel staff, the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], the RN Director of Patient Services, and all offices that keep personnel records
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] keeps complete, accurate, secure personnel records that can be shown to a state surveyor and are kept for the required period.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a personnel record for every employee. The record contains the verification of employment history and qualifications, a signed and dated application, licenses and registrations, performance evaluations, and dates of employment and separation (10 NYCRR §766.11(g)). Health and physical records are kept separately and confidentially. Time and payment records are kept for all personnel (§766.11(h)). Personnel records are retained for 3 years after separation (§766.12(a)(3)). The agency keeps a current listing of all personnel at the principal office and at each branch office (§766.12(a)).

definitions.definition: The file of verifications, qualifications, evaluations, and employment dates for each employee, excluding health records.
The separate file holding health, immunization, TB, and physical records.
The date employment ends by termination or resignation.
A current list of all agency personnel kept at the principal office and each branch.

procedures: HR opens a personnel file for each new hire before the first day of work and uses a standard contents checklist for every file.

Each file contains: the signed and dated application; verification of employment history, references, and qualifications (see PER-02); copies of licenses, registrations, and training certificates; Home Care Registry verification (see PER-09); the signed job description (see PER-10); orientation and in-service records (see PER-03); performance evaluations; and dates of employment and separation (§766.11(g)).

HR completes Form I-9 for each employee within the time required by 8 CFR 274a.2 and keeps it for the federally required period. HR stores I-9 forms in a binder or folder separate from the personnel file.
HR keeps health and physical records in the separate confidential health file described in PER-04. They are never filed in the personnel file.
HR maintains time and payment records for every employee as required by §766.11(h) and 29 CFR 516, including hours worked, rates of pay, and payment dates. See PER-06 and SVC-10.

Personnel files are kept in locked cabinets or in electronic systems with role-based access. Access is limited to the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], the RN Director of Patient Services, HR staff, and others designated in writing. Electronic records must be secure and confidential and be printable on request (§766.12(b)).
HR updates the personnel file within 5 business days of any change such as a new license, a promotion, a new address, or a new evaluation.

HR keeps a current listing of all personnel (name, title, dates of employment, license/registry status). A copy is at the principal office and at each branch office (§766.12(a)). HR updates the listing within 5 business days of each hire or separation.

On separation, HR records the separation date in the file and retains the record for at least 3 years after that date (§766.12(a)(3)). The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] approves destruction in writing, and confidential destruction is documented.
Any DOH surveyor request for personnel records is answered promptly. The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or designee provides the files and keeps a log of what was provided.
The compliance officer audits a sample of personnel files each quarter against the contents checklist. Findings are corrected and reported to the QI Committee.

responsibilities.duty: Builds and maintains files, I-9 forms, the separate health files, and the personnel listing; manages retention and secure disposal.
Ensures records are complete, secure, and available to DOH, and approves destruction.
Provides clinical evaluations, competency records, and license verification for the files.
Performs quarterly file audits.

documentation: Personnel file contents checklist
Form I-9 records
Time and payment records
Current personnel listing for the principal office and each branch
Access list for personnel files
Record destruction approvals
Quarterly file audit reports

policies.title: Wage, Hour and Overtime Compliance
policies.applies_to: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], HR/payroll staff, schedulers, and all hourly employees including home care aides
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] pays all employees at least the legally required minimum wage and overtime, and keeps accurate time and payment records.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] pays home care aides at no less than the home care aide minimum wage under Public Health Law §3614-f: $19.65 per hour in New York City, Long Island, and Westchester, and $18.65 per hour in the rest of the state, from 1/1/2026; and $20.00 and $19.00 from 1/1/2027. The general New York minimum wage is lower, but home care aides must be paid the PHL §3614-f minimum. The agency pays overtime and live-in aide wages as required by the federal Fair Labor Standards Act and 29 CFR Part 552. The agency keeps time and payment records for all personnel (10 NYCRR §766.11(h)) and FLSA records under 29 CFR 516. Wage parity for Medicaid work is handled in PER-11. State-specific rules on 24-hour and 13-hour live-in shifts are confirmed with counsel before the agency applies them.

definitions.definition: The minimum hourly wage that PHL §3614-f requires for home care aides. It is higher than the general state minimum wage and varies by region.
All time an employee is required to work or is on duty, including travel between clients during the workday, as the FLSA defines it.
Pay at 1.5 times the regular rate for hours worked over 40 in a workweek, as required under the FLSA.
An aide who lives at the client's home for extended periods. See SVC-05 for service rules.

procedures: Before hire, HR determines the pay region applicable to the work (New York City, Long Island, and Westchester, or the rest of the state) based on where the aide will provide services. HR records the region in the personnel file. Where there is doubt, HR gets written advice from counsel or NY DOL.
HR sets each home care aide's starting rate at or above the applicable PHL §3614-f minimum: $19.65 or $18.65 per hour from 1/1/2026, and $20.00 or $19.00 per hour from 1/1/2027.

No later than 30 days before each 1/1 change, the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and HR verify the new minimum with NY DOL guidance, update the payroll system, and confirm that every aide's rate is at or above the new minimum. The review is documented.
Payroll staff verify each pay period that no aide's effective hourly rate falls below the applicable minimum. Any shortfall is corrected in the next payroll at the latest, and back pay is paid.

Aides record hours through electronic visit verification and timekeeping (see SVC-10). Payroll compares the recorded hours to scheduled hours and supervisors resolve differences before payroll closes.
Payroll counts as hours worked all time the aide is required to work, including required training, orientation, and travel between clients during the workday. Required training time is paid.
Payroll pays overtime at 1.5 times the regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek, as the FLSA and 29 CFR Part 552 require. Schedulers see weekly hours when assigning shifts.

Before the agency uses live-in or 24-hour shifts, the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] gets written advice from counsel on federal and New York pay rules for those shifts, including sleep and meal time, and records the decision. Pay for these shifts follows the written advice. See SVC-05.
Payroll gives each employee a written wage notice and a pay statement every pay period showing hours, rate, and deductions, as the law requires.

Payroll keeps time and payment records for each employee, including dates, hours worked, rates, and amounts paid (§766.11(h); 29 CFR 516), in the personnel and payroll files, and keeps them for at least the periods in PER-05.

Employees may report pay concerns to the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or the compliance officer without retaliation. Complaints are investigated within 10 business days and corrected pay is issued promptly. Employees are told they may also contact NY DOL.
The compliance officer reviews payroll records at least quarterly against this policy and reports results to the QI Committee and to the governing authority (see GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures wage compliance, verifies annual rate changes, and obtains counsel advice on live-in shift pay.
Set rates by region, process payroll accurately, pay overtime, issue wage notices and statements, and keep records.
Monitor weekly hours and flag likely overtime before assigning shifts.
Audits payroll against the minimum wage and overtime rules each quarter.
Record time accurately and report pay questions promptly.

documentation: Pay region determination for each aide
Annual minimum wage verification and payroll update record
Time and payment records
Pay statements and wage notices
Overtime reports
Counsel advice on live-in shift pay
Wage complaint log and resolution
Quarterly payroll audit reports

policies.title: Staff Conduct and Professional Boundaries
policies.applies_to: All agency personnel, contractors, and volunteers who work with patients or have access to patient information
policies.purpose: To make sure every staff member treats patients with respect, protects patient rights and confidentiality, and keeps professional boundaries.
policies.policy: All [AGENCY NAME] staff must know and uphold patient rights and must protect and promote them (10 NYCRR §766.1(b)). Staff treat every patient with consideration, respect, and full recognition of the patient's dignity and individuality (§766.1(a)(10)). Staff protect the privacy of patient records and release information only as agency policy allows (§766.1(a)(11); see CR-03). Staff conduct is part of the annual performance assessment (§766.11(k)). The agency adopts the specific standards for gifts, social media, and personal relationships set out in this policy.

definitions.definition: The limit that separates a staff member's professional role from the personal, financial, or social life of a patient.
Any behavior that crosses that limit, such as accepting gifts or loans, entering personal or romantic relationships, or sharing patient information.
Any information about a patient's identity, health, care, home, or finances.

procedures: Each employee receives a copy of the Code of Conduct at hire, reviews patient rights (see CR-01) at orientation, and signs an acknowledgment that is placed in the personnel file. The acknowledgment is renewed each year.

Staff treat patients and family members with courtesy and respect, address them as they prefer, protect their privacy during personal care, and do not use abusive, demeaning, or threatening language or conduct.

Staff do not accept gifts, tips, money, loans, or items of value from patients or family members, and do not ask for them, except as allowed by CR-04. Any offer is reported to the supervisor the same day and recorded.

Staff do not borrow money or property from patients, sell items or services to them, handle their money or property except as the plan of care allows, or be named in a patient's will or as a beneficiary. See CR-04.

Staff do not enter personal, romantic, or sexual relationships with a patient. Staff do not provide personal services outside the plan of care, and do not take on private-pay work for agency patients outside the agency.

Staff do not share patient information with anyone who does not need it for care or business purposes. Staff do not post patient names, photos, addresses, or care details on social media or messaging apps. See CR-03.
Staff do not use a patient's phone, computer, vehicle, or supplies for personal purposes, and do not use patient information for personal gain.
Staff do not provide care while impaired by alcohol or drugs, and do not use tobacco, alcohol, or illegal drugs in a patient's home.
Staff do not bring friends, family members, or children to the patient's home during work hours.
Staff report any suspected abuse, neglect, or exploitation as SAF-01 requires, and any boundary concern or offer of a gift to the supervisor the same day.

Staff who see conduct that may violate this policy report it to the RN Director of Patient Services or the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME]. Reports can also be made to the compliance officer. No one is retaliated against for a good-faith report.

The RN Director of Patient Services or the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews each report within 2 business days. A reported boundary violation involving possible abuse, neglect, or exploitation is handled under SAF-01. The investigation is documented.

Violations lead to corrective action up to and including termination, depending on the facts. Where a patient may be at risk, the staff member is removed from the patient's care immediately and the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] decides on any required reports (see REC-02).

The annual performance evaluation includes a conduct section covering respect for patients, boundary compliance, and confidentiality (§766.11(k); see PER-10). The evaluator records any conduct concerns.

responsibilities.duty: Know and follow this policy, protect patient rights and information, avoid boundary violations, and report concerns.
Reviews boundary concerns, directs removal from a case where needed, and includes conduct in supervisory reviews.
Enforces the Code of Conduct, takes corrective action, and makes any required reports.
Obtains annual acknowledgments and files conduct-related documentation.
Receives confidential reports and tracks trends for the QI Committee.

documentation: Signed Code of Conduct acknowledgment (at hire and annually)
Orientation record showing patient rights training
Gift offer and boundary concern reports
Investigation notes and outcome of each report
Corrective action records
Annual performance evaluation conduct section

policies.title: Caregiver Photo Identification and Badges
policies.applies_to: All caregivers (personal care aides and any other personnel) who provide services in patients' homes, and the administrative staff who issue and collect identification
policies.purpose: To make sure every patient and household can verify who is entering the home, and that no former employee keeps agency identification, as required by 10 NYCRR §766.2(a)(4).
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires every caregiver who works in a patient's home to display proper and current agency identification. The identification must show the caregiver's name, title, a current photograph and the name of the agency. Identification is issued before the caregiver's first patient contact and is returned to the agency when employment ends. Expired, damaged, altered or outdated identification is replaced promptly. The agency keeps an identification issue and return log.

definitions.definition: A photo identification card issued by [AGENCY NAME] showing the caregiver's name, title, current photograph and the agency name.
Unexpired, unaltered, with a photograph that still looks like the caregiver, and showing the caregiver's present title.
Any end of employment or assignment, whether by resignation, termination, end of contract or other reason.

procedures: The Human Resources designee takes a clear, front-facing photograph of each new caregiver during orientation, after identity has been verified under PER-02.
The HR designee prepares the badge showing the caregiver's full name, job title (for example, Personal Care Aide), the current photograph and the agency name, [AGENCY NAME].
No caregiver is scheduled for a first patient visit until the badge has been issued and the caregiver has signed for it.
At issue, the HR designee enters the caregiver's name, title, badge number or issue date, and the caregiver's signature in the Identification Issue and Return Log.
The caregiver is instructed to wear the badge visibly at all times while in a patient's home, at the start of each visit, and to show it to the patient or household member on arrival.
The caregiver must be willing to let the patient or a family member read the badge and call the agency at [PHONE] to confirm identity. Staff must not discourage or take offense at this.
Caregivers may not lend, copy, alter or cover any part of the badge, and may not use the badge for any purpose other than agency work.

If a badge is lost, stolen, damaged or illegible, the caregiver notifies the supervisor or the office the same day. The HR designee deactivates the old badge number in the log and issues a replacement as soon as possible.
The HR designee replaces the badge promptly when the caregiver's name or title changes, when the photograph is no longer a good likeness, or when the badge is worn or altered.
The HR designee reviews the log every quarter for badges that are expired, damaged or in need of a new photograph, and for any badge issued to a person who is no longer active.
On separation, the supervisor or HR designee collects the badge at the exit conference or by prepaid mail or courier within [NUMBER] business days, and records the return date in the log.
If a badge is not returned, the HR designee documents at least two written or recorded attempts to retrieve it, marks the badge as void in the log, and tells the Administrator.

For a badge that is outstanding after separation, the Administrator decides whether the patients served by that caregiver must be told that the person no longer works for the agency, and the notice is documented.

The RN Director of Patient Services or supervising RN checks during in-home supervisory visits that the caregiver is wearing current identification, and records any deficiency in the supervisory visit report.
The Administrator reviews the identification log findings at least once a year as part of the personnel policy review.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures this policy is carried out; decides on notices to patients when a badge is not returned; reviews the log annually.
Takes photographs, prepares and issues badges, maintains the Identification Issue and Return Log, collects badges at separation, and follows up on unreturned badges.

responsibilities.role: RN Director of Patient Services / supervising RN
responsibilities.duty: Verifies during in-home visits that caregivers display current identification and reports deficiencies.
Wears the badge visibly in the home, shows it to patients, reports a lost or damaged badge the same day, and returns it at separation.

documentation: Identification Issue and Return Log (issue date, replacement date, return date, deactivation date)
Signed badge receipt in the personnel record
Record of attempts to retrieve unreturned badges
Supervisory visit report notes on identification

policies.title: Home Care Worker Registry Entry and Maintenance
policies.applies_to: Designated registry users, Human Resources and scheduling staff, and all home health aides and personal care aides
policies.purpose: To make sure every aide's information is in the NYS Home Care Worker Registry, that only authorized staff enter registry data, and that no aide who must be posted works before posting, as required by 10 NYCRR Part 403, Public Health Law §3613 and 10 NYCRR §766.11(b).
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is an Article 36 licensed agency and complies with 10 NYCRR Part 403. The agency designates at least two individuals to access and enter data in the Home Care Worker Registry and gives DOH their names and contact information. Only designated individuals submit registry data. Before hire, the agency reviews the aide's registry profile and training materials. The agency confirms that the PHL §3613(3)(a)-(f) information is in the registry. An aide who completed a state-approved training program on or after September 25, 2009 does not provide services until the aide has been posted to the registry. Within 10 business days after an aide begins providing services, the agency updates the registry with employment information including the start date.

definitions.definition: The statewide registry established under Public Health Law §3613 and maintained by DOH, holding information about workers who completed state-approved home care training programs.
A staff member the agency has designated to access and enter data in the registry under 10 NYCRR §403.3(a).
The registry record for an aide, showing the training program and other required information.
Appearing in the registry as a person who completed an approved training program.

procedures: The Administrator designates at least two individuals ([REGISTRY DESIGNEE 1] and [REGISTRY DESIGNEE 2]) to access and enter registry data. The designation is in writing and kept in the compliance file.
The Administrator gives DOH the names and contact information of the designated individuals, and sends updated information to DOH whenever a designee is added, replaced or leaves.

Access credentials are personal. Designated individuals may not share logins, and no one else may submit data to the registry. The Administrator removes a designee's access on the day the designation ends.

Before a candidate is offered an aide position, a designated individual reviews the candidate's registry aide profile and the training materials the candidate provides, including the training certificate if available.

The designated individual confirms that the training was given by a program approved by DOH or the State Education Department (SED), and records the program name, completion date and result of the review on the Registry Verification Checklist.

The designated individual confirms that the PHL §3613(3)(a)-(f) information is in the registry for the aide. If it is missing or inconsistent, HR notifies the aide and the training program and does not schedule the aide for patient care until the issue is resolved.

For an aide trained in a state-approved program on or after September 25, 2009, HR confirms that the aide is posted in the registry before the aide is given any patient assignment. If the aide is not posted, the scheduler may not assign the aide.
HR verifies any advanced home health aide status shown in the registry, and any limitation or revocation of that status, before assigning duties.

On the aide's first day of providing services to a patient, HR records the start date. The designated individual updates the registry with the employment information, including the start date, within 10 business days after the aide begins providing services.
The designated individual prints or saves a confirmation of each registry update and places it in the personnel record with the date entered and the initials of the person who entered it.
When an aide's employment with the agency ends, or other employment information changes, the designated individual updates the registry as the registry requires, and records the date.
Each month, a designated individual compares the active aide roster and payroll with registry entries, and corrects any aide whose start date or employment information is missing or late.

The RN Director of Patient Services and the scheduling supervisor are told when an aide is not posted or has a registry problem, and the scheduler blocks that aide from assignments until the Administrator clears the hold.
The Administrator reviews this policy and the registry monitoring results during the annual personnel policy review under §766.11(a) and reports any late or missing entries to the QI Committee.

responsibilities.duty: Designates at least two registry users, notifies DOH of their names and contact information, ensures compliance with Part 403, and clears registry holds.
Review aide profiles, enter and update registry data within required time frames, and keep confirmations.
Collects training documents, completes the Registry Verification Checklist, and keeps personnel records.
Does not assign any aide who is not posted or is on hold.
Confirms aide qualifications before assignment and acts on registry-related holds.

documentation: Written designation of registry users and the notice sent to DOH
Registry Verification Checklist and copy of the aide profile and training certificate
Registry update confirmation with start date and date entered
Monthly registry-to-payroll reconciliation
Record of registry holds and their resolution

policies.title: Job Descriptions and Annual Performance Evaluation
policies.applies_to: All agency employees and contracted personnel, and the supervisors who evaluate them
policies.purpose: To make sure each position has a current written job description and that each employee's performance is assessed at least annually, as required by 10 NYCRR §766.11(j) and (k).
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a current written job description for every position. Each job description states the position's responsibilities and its education and experience requirements. At least once a year the agency assesses the performance and effectiveness of all personnel. For personnel who provide care in the home, the assessment includes at least one in-home visit to observe performance, where applicable. Evaluations are kept in the personnel record.

definitions.definition: A written statement of a position's responsibilities, reporting relationship, and required education and experience.
A written evaluation of each employee's performance and effectiveness completed at least once every 12 months.
A visit by a qualified supervisor, usually the RN, to watch the employee perform care in the patient's home, with the patient's agreement.

procedures: The Administrator and RN Director of Patient Services write a job description for every position, including the Administrator, RN Director of Patient Services, supervising RNs, personal care aides, home health aides (if used), schedulers and office staff.
Each job description states responsibilities, reporting relationship, required education and experience, licensure or certification, and physical and health requirements for the position.
The aide job description reflects only the tasks allowed under SVC-01, and the nursing supervisory job description reflects the supervision duties in SVC-07 and §766.5.
At hire, HR gives the employee the job description. The employee signs and dates an acknowledgment, which goes in the personnel record.

The Administrator reviews every job description at least annually as part of the personnel policy review, and revises it when duties change. Superseded versions are kept with the date of change under GOV-03.
HR keeps a performance evaluation calendar showing each employee's hire date and the date the annual assessment is due, and tells supervisors 30 days before it is due.
Each employee is evaluated by their direct supervisor using the agency's performance evaluation form, which measures performance against the job description.

For aides, the RN supervisor schedules at least one in-home observation visit within each evaluation year. The RN, with the patient's agreement, watches the aide perform assigned tasks and checks use of the plan of care, infection control, documentation, professional boundaries and communication.
For aides, the supervisor also considers attendance and punctuality, EVV compliance, patient and family feedback, complaints, incident reports and completion of in-service training under PER-03.
The RN records the in-home observation findings in the evaluation, with the date of the visit, the patient's initials or record number, and the observer's name and title.
The supervisor reviews the written evaluation with the employee within [NUMBER] days of the assessment. The employee signs it and may add comments.
Where an evaluation shows deficiencies, the supervisor writes a corrective action plan with dates, arranges re-training or a follow-up observation, and records the outcome.
If an aide's skills are found unsafe, the RN Director of Patient Services removes the aide from patient care duties until re-training and competency are documented under PER-03.
HR files the signed evaluation, observation record and any corrective action plan in the personnel record, separate from confidential health records.
The Administrator reports the percentage of evaluations completed on time to the QI Committee each quarter.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures job descriptions exist and are current, ensures evaluations are completed, and reports completion rates to the QI Committee.
Ensures nursing and aide job descriptions are accurate and that in-home observation visits are done for aides.
Complete evaluations on time, perform observations, review results with employees and follow up on deficiencies.
Maintains job descriptions, tracks due dates, and files signed documents.
Signs acknowledgment of the job description and takes part in evaluation and observation.

documentation: Current job description for each position and revision history
Employee's signed job description acknowledgment
Annual performance evaluation form, signed and dated
In-home observation visit record
Corrective action plans and follow-up documentation
Evaluation due-date tracking calendar

policies.title: Home Care Aide Minimum Wage and Wage Parity (Downstate Medicaid)
policies.applies_to: Payroll, HR, billing and management staff, and all home care aides paid by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure home care aides are paid at least the New York home care aide minimum wage and, for Medicaid-funded work in the New York City metropolitan counties, the wage parity total compensation required by Public Health Law §3614-c.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] pays every home care aide at least the home care aide minimum wage required by Public Health Law §3614-f, regardless of payer. For Medicaid-funded home care in New York City, Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester counties, the agency also provides total compensation equal to the home care aide minimum plus the wage parity benefit portion required by Public Health Law §3614-c. The agency files the annual wage parity certification with an independently audited statement and keeps the records for 10 years. The agency also follows the federal rules on domestic service employees at 29 CFR Part 552.

definitions.definition: The minimum hourly wage under PHL §3614-f. In 2026 it is $19.65 in New York City, Long Island (Nassau and Suffolk) and Westchester, and $18.65 in the rest of the state. It rises to $20.00 and $19.00 on January 1, 2027.
The requirement that, for Medicaid-funded home care in New York City, Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester, total compensation equals the home care aide minimum plus a benefit portion.
$2.54 per hour in New York City and $1.67 per hour in Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester, effective January 1, 2024. It may be paid as supplemental wages or as qualifying benefits.
Wages plus the benefit portion. In 2026 this is $22.19 per hour in New York City and $21.32 per hour in Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester.

procedures: The Administrator assigns payroll compliance to [PAYROLL/COMPLIANCE DESIGNEE], who keeps a rate table showing for each county served the applicable home care aide minimum wage and, for Medicaid work, the wage parity benefit portion.

Each January, and whenever the law changes, the designee updates the rate table, confirms the current figures against Department of Labor and DOH published notices, and records the date of the check. The 2026 figures are $19.65 / $18.65 minimum and $2.54 / $1.67 benefit portion; the 2027 minimums are $20.00 / $19.00.

The payroll system is set up so that no aide's regular hourly rate is below the minimum for the county where the aide's patient lives. The designee checks the system settings before each rate change takes effect.
At each pay run, payroll flags any aide whose rate is below the applicable minimum. The designee corrects the rate and pays any shortfall before the pay date.
For each aide, payroll tracks Medicaid hours worked in New York City, Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester separately from other hours, using EVV and timekeeping records from SVC-10.

For Medicaid hours in those counties, the designee confirms that total compensation meets the wage parity amount, whether paid in wages, supplemental pay or qualifying benefits, and records how each aide's benefit portion is provided.
The designee keeps benefit documents, plan invoices and proof of payment that show how each benefit portion was funded and delivered.

Each January the Billing Manager checks whether each MLTC plan contract and rate passes through the new minimum wage and benefit increase. Any gap is reported in writing to the Administrator, and the agency raises it with the plan.

The Billing Manager records the plan's reply and, where a plan will not cover the increase, the Administrator decides whether to renegotiate or limit new referrals. The agency does not lower an aide's pay to make up the gap.
Aides are told in writing of their hourly rate, the benefit portion that applies to them, and their overtime rights. The employee's acknowledgment goes in the personnel record.

The designee prepares the annual wage parity certification and engages an independent auditor to prepare the audited statement. The Administrator reviews and signs the certification before it is filed.
The Administrator files the certification and audited statement by the required date, and records the filing date and confirmation in the compliance calendar (see REC-02).

Payroll, benefit and parity records are kept for 10 years, in line with the wage parity requirement, and are available for DOH, Department of Labor or plan review. General time and payment records follow PER-05 and REC-02.

An aide who believes he or she was underpaid reports it to the Administrator, who investigates within [NUMBER] business days, pays any amount owed with the next payroll, and documents the finding. No employee is disciplined for raising a wage concern.
The Administrator reports annually to the QI Committee and the governing authority on wage compliance, audit findings and plan pass-through status.

responsibilities.duty: Signs the annual wage parity certification, ensures timely filing, and addresses any underpayment.
Maintains the rate table, sets and checks payroll rates, tracks Medicaid hours by county, and gathers audit and benefit records.
Checks each January whether MLTC contracts pass through wage increases and reports gaps.
Prepares the independently audited statement for the annual wage parity filing.
Gives aides written notice of pay and benefit information and files acknowledgments.

documentation: County rate table with annual check dates
Payroll registers showing rate, hours and total compensation
Medicaid hours by county report
Benefit plan documents and proof of payment
Annual wage parity certification and independently audited statement
Record of MLTC pass-through reviews and plan correspondence
Employee pay notices and acknowledgments
Wage complaint investigation records
All wage parity records retained for 10 years

policies.title: Patient Records and Retention
policies.applies_to: All employees and contracted staff who create, use, store, release or destroy patient records, in paper or electronic form
policies.purpose: To make sure each patient has a complete, confidential, secure record that is kept for the required time and is available to DOH, as required by 10 NYCRR §766.6 and §766.12(b).
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a confidential record for every patient. The record contains the items required by 10 NYCRR §766.6(a). Records are kept securely for at least six years after discharge and are available to DOH. For a minor patient, records are kept for six years after discharge or three years after the patient turns 18, whichever is longer. Written procedures safeguard records against loss or unauthorized access and control their use, removal and release. Electronic records are secure, confidential and can be printed on request. If the agency closes, the governing authority arranges for storage and access and notifies DOH in writing where the records are kept.

definitions.definition: The confidential record of each patient's care, in paper or electronic form, containing the required contents under 10 NYCRR §766.6(a).
A signed and dated entry made after each visit or phone contact.
The final record entry summarizing services, reason for discharge, and the patient's status and referrals at discharge.
Giving a copy of or access to record information to someone outside the agency.

procedures: On acceptance of a patient, the intake nurse opens a record and enters identifying data. The record is assigned a unique number and stored in the agency's electronic system or in a locked file in the office at [ADDRESS].

The record contains: identifying data; medical orders; nursing assessments; the plan of care; signed and dated progress notes after each visit or phone contact; RN supervisory reports; aide observations and activity sheets; documentation of accidents and incidents; documentation that the patient received rights information; and a discharge summary.
The RN confirms that the patient or representative signed the rights acknowledgment (CR-01) and files it in the record at the start of service.

Aides complete their activity sheets or EVV tasks and observations at each visit, and submit them by the end of the visit or by [TIME] the next business day. The supervisor reviews them at least [FREQUENCY].

RNs and other staff sign and date every entry, record the date of the visit or contact, and chart changes in condition promptly. Corrections are made by a single line through the entry with the date and initials, and nothing is erased or obliterated.
Accidents and incidents are documented in the patient's record and reported under SAF-02. The record notes the date and the actions taken.

The Medical Records designee checks each record at least [FREQUENCY] for completeness and tells the RN Director of Patient Services about missing items, which are completed within [NUMBER] business days.

Paper records are kept in locked cabinets in a room that is locked outside business hours. Electronic records require individual passwords, role-based access, automatic log-off and an audit trail. Staff may not share passwords.

Staff access only the records they need to do their jobs. Records are not removed from the office except as the supervisor authorizes for care delivery, and removal is logged with the person's name, date and return date. Records are not left unattended in vehicles or public places.

The Medical Records designee releases information only as allowed by CR-03 and applicable law, with a valid authorization or other lawful basis. Each release is logged with the date, the recipient, the information released and the staff member who released it.
The agency gives DOH surveyors and other authorized officials access to records on request, and tells the Administrator at once when such a request is made.
The Administrator confirms that the electronic record system can print a complete copy of any record on request, and tests this at least once a year.
Electronic records are backed up at least daily, and the backup is stored securely off site or in an approved cloud service under a written agreement. Restoration is tested at least once a year.

On discharge, the RN completes the discharge summary under SVC-12 and the record is closed. The Medical Records designee enters the discharge date and the earliest destruction date in the retention log.

Records are retained for at least six years after discharge. For a minor, the record is kept six years after discharge or three years after the patient reaches age 18, whichever is longer. A record needed for an open complaint, investigation, audit or legal hold is not destroyed until the Administrator releases it in writing.

At the end of the retention period, the Administrator approves destruction. Paper is cross-cut shredded and electronic records are permanently erased. Each destruction is logged with the date, record number and method, but not the clinical content.
If the agency plans to close, the governing authority makes written arrangements for secure storage and continued access for patients and DOH, and notifies DOH in writing where the records are kept.
The agency keeps its records policies and related documentation for at least six years, in line with 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2).
The QI Committee reviews a random sample of current and recently discharged patients' records at least four times a year under GOV-04 and reports record deficiencies to the governing authority.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the records system is secure and compliant, approves destruction and legal holds, and carries out closure arrangements with the governing authority.
Ensures records are complete, timely and accurate, and that RN and aide documentation meets standards.
Maintains record files, retention and release logs, completeness checks and destruction logs.
Document each visit or contact accurately, sign and date entries, and protect the privacy of record information.
Arranges storage and access to records and notifies DOH in writing if the agency closes.

documentation: Complete patient care record containing every item required by 10 NYCRR §766.6(a)
Record release log
Record removal log
Retention and destruction log
Electronic system access audit logs and backup test results
Record completeness audit results
Written notice to DOH of record storage location, if the agency closes

policies.title: Required Reports to the State
policies.applies_to: Administrator, RN Director of Patient Services, billing, payroll and compliance staff, and the governing authority
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] submits every report and filing that DOH and New York law require, on time and accurately.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] promptly submits all records and reports that DOH requires. These include annual statistical summaries of services and reimbursement and an ownership list, annual registration under Public Health Law §3605-b, cost reports when DOH requires them under Public Health Law §3612, the weekly HERDS survey, the annual wage parity certification and audited statement under Public Health Law §3614-c, and any management contract or franchise proposals. The Administrator keeps a compliance calendar and is responsible for timely, accurate filing.

definitions.definition: The DOH weekly survey on which LHCSAs report patient census by licensed county. The reporting window opens Tuesday at 8:00 a.m. and closes Thursday at 2:00 p.m.
The yearly report of services provided and reimbursement received, submitted on forms DOH provides.
The annual list of owners: stockholders for a for-profit agency, or directors and officers for a not-for-profit agency.
A financial report that DOH requires agencies to file under Public Health Law §3612.
The agency's schedule of all report due dates, the person responsible, and the date each was filed.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a compliance calendar listing each required report, its due date, the responsible person, a backup person, and the date filed. The calendar is reviewed at the weekly management meeting.

For the weekly HERDS survey, the Administrator designates [HERDS DESIGNEE] and a backup. The designee compiles the patient census by licensed county from the scheduling system on [DAY], and verifies it against the active patient roster.

The HERDS designee submits the survey in the window that opens Tuesday at 8:00 a.m. and closes Thursday at 2:00 p.m., and saves the confirmation. If a submission is missed or in error, the designee immediately contacts DOH at hcstatrpts@health.ny.gov, and the Administrator is told the same day.

Each year, the Administrator compiles the annual statistical summary of services and reimbursement from billing and clinical records, completes the DOH form, and has the RN Director of Patient Services review the service data before filing.

The Administrator prepares the annual list of owners (stockholders for a for-profit agency, directors and officers for a not-for-profit agency), checks it against corporate records, and submits it to DOH with the annual summary.

The Administrator completes annual registration of the agency under Public Health Law §3605-b by the date set by DOH. The agency may not operate or be paid if it is unregistered, and late registration carries a penalty of $500 per month. Missing two registration periods can lead to revocation. The registration confirmation is kept in the compliance file.

When DOH notifies the agency that a cost report is required under Public Health Law §3612, the Administrator logs the notice date, assigns the report to the billing and finance staff, and files it within 90 days of the notice. If DOH finds errors, the agency corrects them within the 30-day correction window.
For the annual wage parity filing, the Administrator signs the annual certification and files it with the independently audited statement, as described in PER-11, and records the filing date.

Before the agency enters a management contract or franchise agreement, the Administrator submits the proposal to DOH at least 60 days before the proposed effective date and does not put it into effect without the Commissioner's prior written consent (see GOV-06).

If the agency uses advanced home health aides, the RN Director of Patient Services notifies DOH when a supervising RN fails to meet the advanced home health aide supervision requirements. The report is made promptly and documented.

The Administrator submits other records and reports that DOH requires promptly, and responds to DOH requests by the date given. A request that cannot be met in time is discussed with DOH before the due date, and the discussion is documented.

Before filing, a second person reviews every report for accuracy and for consistency with agency records. The Administrator signs off, and a copy and proof of submission are kept in the compliance file.

If a late or incorrect filing is found, the Administrator corrects it as soon as possible, tells DOH if required, documents the cause and corrective action, and reports it to the governing authority and the QI Committee.
Filed reports and proofs of submission are retained under REC-03 and the retention schedule in 10 NYCRR §766.12.
Each quarter the Administrator reports to the governing authority on the status of required reports, any late filings, and upcoming deadlines.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the compliance calendar, signs and files required reports, and corrects any late or inaccurate filings.
Compiles and submits the weekly HERDS census by licensed county within the Tuesday-to-Thursday window.
Verifies service and census data and notifies DOH of any supervision failure that must be reported.
Prepare reimbursement data, cost reports and wage parity documents.
Receives quarterly status reports on required filings and ensures the agency has the resources to comply.

documentation: Compliance calendar with due dates, assignments and filing dates
Weekly HERDS submission confirmations
Annual statistical summary and ownership list as filed
Annual registration confirmation
Cost report notices, filings and correspondence with DOH
Wage parity certification and audited statement as filed
Management contract or franchise proposals and DOH consent
Corrective action records for late or incorrect filings

policies.title: Agency Records on File, Branch Offices and Retention Schedule
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] administrative, personnel, patient, financial and governance records, at the principal New York State office and at every branch office, in hard copy or electronic form.
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] keeps the records the New York State Department of Health (DOH) requires at the principal office and at each branch office, keeps each record for at least the minimum period, and can produce any record promptly on request. The same applies to electronic records.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps at its principal New York State office the license, organizational documents, assumed-name certificate, patient-care contracts, governing-authority and quality assurance bylaws, current operating policies, a current patient roster and a list of all personnel (10 NYCRR §766.12(a)(1)). Each branch office keeps current policies, a personnel list and its patient records (§766.12(a)(2)). Records are retained for at least the minimum periods in this policy: governing-authority and committee minutes, 3 years; patient-care financial records, 3 years; personnel records, 3 years after separation; complaint and grievance records, 3 years after resolution; and patient care records as required by §766.6 (§766.12(a)(3)). Records may be kept in hard copy or electronically. Electronic records must be secure, confidential and printable on request (§766.12(b)). [AGENCY NAME] submits promptly all records and reports DOH requires (§766.12(a)). Where a payer contract or another law requires a longer retention period, the longer period applies. Records are not destroyed while a survey, complaint, audit, investigation or legal matter is open.

definitions.definition: The agency's main office in New York State, at [ADDRESS], where the records listed in §766.12(a)(1) are kept.
Any additional agency site approved by DOH. It keeps the records listed in §766.12(a)(2).

The confidential record kept for each patient under §766.6, including identifying data, orders, assessments, the plan of care, progress notes, RN supervisory reports, aide observations and activity sheets, incident documentation, rights acknowledgment and the discharge summary.
The minimum time a record must be kept before it may be destroyed, counted from the trigger event stated in the retention schedule.
Any record created, stored or transmitted in digital form, including scheduling, timekeeping, clinical and personnel systems.

procedures: The Administrator, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], is responsible for the agency records inventory. The RN Director of Patient Services is responsible for the clinical record content listed in the inventory.

The Administrator keeps a Principal Office Records Index. It lists each of these items and where it is filed: the agency license; the certificate of incorporation or partnership agreement; the assumed-name certificate; patient-care contracts; governing-authority bylaws; quality assurance bylaws; current operating policies; the current patient roster; and the list of all personnel.
The Administrator checks the Principal Office Records Index each quarter and signs and dates the check. Any missing or outdated item is replaced within 10 business days and noted on the index.

The current patient roster and the list of all personnel are updated at least weekly, and immediately after any admission, discharge or hire. Each update shows the date and the name of the person who made it.

Each branch office keeps a Branch Records Index covering current policies, the personnel list, and the patient records and roster for patients served from that branch. The branch manager reviews the index quarterly and sends the signed review to the Administrator.

When the policy manual is revised under GOV-03, the Administrator sends the current version to every branch within 5 business days. Each branch removes the superseded version and marks it as superseded, then files it per the retention schedule.

Patient care records are kept securely for at least 6 years after discharge. For a patient who is a minor, the record is kept until 6 years after discharge or 3 years after the patient reaches age 18, whichever is longer (§766.6(b), (c)).
Governing-authority and committee minutes, including QI Committee minutes, are kept for at least 3 years from the date of the meeting.
Patient-care financial records (service agreements, billing, claims and payment records) are kept for at least 3 years. Staff apply any longer period required by a payer contract or law.

Personnel records are kept for at least 3 years after the employee's separation. The Administrator records the separation date on the personnel file cover so the destruction date can be calculated (see PER-05).
Complaint and grievance records are kept for at least 3 years after the complaint is resolved. The Administrator records the resolution date in the complaint log (see CR-02).

Each year, the Administrator prepares a Records Disposal List showing records that have passed their retention period, the retention rule applied and the destruction date. The Administrator and the RN Director of Patient Services review and sign it before any destruction. No record is destroyed if it is subject to a hold because of a survey, complaint, audit, investigation or legal matter. The Administrator documents each hold and its release.

Records approved for destruction are shredded or, for electronic files, permanently erased. A Certificate of Destruction is kept permanently. It lists the record types, date ranges, method, date and the person who carried out the destruction.

Paper records are kept in locked cabinets or a locked room. Only staff with a job-related need may access them. Staff may not remove records from the office except as allowed in REC-01 and CR-03, and any removal is logged. Electronic systems use individual user IDs, role-based access, passwords and activity logs. The Administrator reviews user access at least quarterly and removes access on the day an employee separates.

Electronic records are backed up on a regular schedule, and the backup is stored securely. The Administrator tests at least once a year that a sample of electronic patient and personnel records can be retrieved and printed.

On a request from DOH, staff provide the requested records, in hard copy where asked, promptly. Staff print electronic records on request and do not alter them. The Administrator logs each request, the records provided, the date and the staff member who supplied them.

The Administrator sends DOH the records and reports it requires on time, including the annual statistical summaries of services and reimbursement and the ownership list (see REC-02). The Administrator keeps a copy of each submission.

If the agency closes, the governing authority arranges for storage of patient records and for access to them. It notifies DOH in writing where the records will be kept (§766.6(d)). The Administrator keeps a copy of the notice and the storage arrangements.

responsibilities.duty: Approves this policy. Ensures resources for secure record keeping. Arranges record storage and access and notifies DOH in writing if the agency closes.

Maintains the Principal Office Records Index, the retention schedule, the Records Disposal List and the destruction certificates. Oversees branch compliance, electronic system security and responses to DOH record requests.
Makes sure patient care records are complete under §766.6, are retained for the required period, and are accessible only to authorized staff. Co-signs the disposal of clinical records.
Maintains the Branch Records Index. Keeps current policies, the personnel list and patient records at the branch. Sends the quarterly review to the Administrator.
File, update and retrieve records as directed. Follow access and removal controls. Report any lost, misplaced or improperly accessed record to the Administrator immediately.
Reviews record-keeping audit results, including missing items on the indexes, and recommends corrective action.

documentation: Principal Office Records Index with quarterly review signatures
Branch Records Indexes and quarterly branch reviews
Current patient roster and personnel list, with update dates
Retention schedule and annual Records Disposal List with signatures
Certificates of Destruction (kept permanently)
Record hold and release log
Record removal and release log
Electronic system access review and annual retrieval test results
Log of DOH record requests and responses
Copies of reports and statistical summaries submitted to DOH
Closure notice to DOH and storage arrangements, if applicable
